\section{Applications to the smooth cohomology of $\Diff_v(M)$}\label{sec2233}

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem~\ref{main1}.
The key ingredient will be the Chern--Simons invariant, which we briefly review in
Subsection~\ref{sssdd}.
In Subsection~\ref{sec3a884}, we give the proof of Theorem \ref{main1}, and in Section \ref{hyp11}, we similarly discuss hyperbolic case.
Finally, in Section \ref{sec293392}, 
we discuss obstruction of smoothness of cocycles on $\Ss\neq\{G^{n+1}\}$. 
\subsection{Review: Cheeger--Chern--Simons cocycles}\label{sssdd}

We begin by recalling the definition of the Chern--Simons form.
Let $G$ be a Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, and let
$E\to M$ be a principal $G$-bundle.
Let $  P\colon\mathfrak g^k\to\R$
be a symmetric $k$-linear map which is invariant under the diagonal adjoint action
$G\curvearrowright\mathfrak g^k$.
Let $t \in \R.$
Given two connections $\omega_0,\omega_1\in\AAA^1(E;\mathfrak g)$, we consider the
affine interpolation
$
 \omega_t:=(1- t)\,\omega_0 + t\,\omega_1$
and denote by
$
 \Omega_t:=d\omega_t+\tfrac12[\omega_t,\omega_t]$ its curvature.
By the basic results of Chern--Weil theory, the $2k$-form
$P(\Omega_t,\dots,\Omega_t)$ is closed and its de Rham cohomology class is independent of $t$.
The \emph{Chern--Simons $(2k-1)$-form} associated with $P$ and the pair of connections 
$\omega_0,\omega_1$ is defined by
\[
  T_P(\omega_0,\omega_1)
  :=k\int_0^1 P\bigl(\omega_0 -\omega_1,\Omega_t,\dots,\Omega_t\bigr)\,dt
  \in\Omega^{2k-1}(M).
\]
It satisfies the transgression identity
\[
  P(\Omega_0,\dots,\Omega_0)-P(\Omega_1,\dots,\Omega_1)
  =d\bigl( T_P(\omega_0,\omega_1)\bigr).
\]

If $M$ is a closed $(2k-1)$-dimensional manifold, the (relative) \emph{Chern--Simons invariant} for two connections $\omega_0,\omega_1$ is
the integral $
 \int_M T_P(\omega_0,\omega_1) \in \R$. 

There are two natural issues here.
First, this integral is in general not gauge invariant.
However, for suitable normalizations of $P$, the integral $ \int_M T_P(\omega_0,\omega_1) \in \R/\Z$ modulo $\Z$ is often well
defined and becomes gauge invariant. 
Second, one has to choose the reference connection $\omega_0$.
Two standard choices are the following:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $E$ is the trivial bundle $G\times M$, one often takes $\omega_0$ to be the
      trivial connection.
\item If $G=\SO(2k-1)$ and $E$ is the principal frame bundle associated with the tangent
      bundle of $M$, one takes $\omega_0$ to be the Levi-Civita connection of a fixed
      Riemannian metric on $M$.
\end{enumerate}

Next, we recall the notion of \emph{Cheeger--Chern--Simons cocycles} (CCS cocycles);
see \cite{CS}.
For each group $G$ endowed with the discrete topology we fix an Eilenberg--MacLane space
$K(G,1)$.
If $G=\pi_1(M)$, we fix a classifying map $
 \iota: M \ra K(\pi_1(M),1).$
Given a group homomorphism $f:\pi_1(M)\to G$, there is an induced cellular map
$f_*\circ\iota :M \to K(G,1)$, unique up to homotopy.
In particular, the fundamental class $[M]\in H_{2k-1}(M )$ has a well-defined image
\[
 f_*[M]\in H_{2k-1}(K(G,1) )\cong H_{2k-1}^{\rm gr}(G ).
\]
On the other hand, the basic theory of flat bundles associates to $f$ a principal
$G$-bundle $E_f\to M$ endowed with a flat connection $\omega_f$, up to conjugacy.

In the above situation, a group $(2k-1)$-cocycle $c_P^{\mathrm{CS}}: G^{2k} \to \R/\Z$ is called a
\emph{Cheeger--Chern--Simons cocycle} \cite{CS} for $P$ if for every group homomorphism
$f:\pi_1(M)\to G$ there exists a connection $\omega_0$ on $E_f$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{csinv}
  \int_M T_P (\omega_0,\omega_f) 
  = \bigl\langle [c_P^{\mathrm{CS}}], f_* [M]\bigr\rangle
  \in\R/\Z.
\end{equation}
In situations (i) and (ii) above, the reference connection $\omega_0$ is chosen as
indicated: trivial in case~(i) and Levi-Civita in case~(ii), respectively.

In general, the existence of CCS cocycles depends on the choice of $E$, $G$ and $P$, and
even when they exist it is a subtle problem to decide on which subset $S_{2k-1} \subset G^{2k}$ such a
cocycle can be chosen to be smooth.
The history of this problem is long and intricate, so we confine ourselves to quoting two
typical results, which we use later.
\begin{exa}\label{ex21}
Let $k=2n$ and $G={\rm SO}(4n)$, and let $P$ be the $n$-th Pontryagin polynomial.
Set $K:= {\rm SO}(4n-1)$; then $G/K\cong S^{4n-1}$.
Let $\lambda$ denote the standard volume form ${\rm vol}(S^{4n-1})$ on $S^{4n-1}$.
By Proposition~\ref{312} we can construct a filling $\sigma$ and obtain a
group cocycle $ \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}\bigl({\rm vol}(S^{4n-1})\bigr) : G^{4n} \ra \R/\Z.$
According to \cite{DK,Dup3}, this cocycle is a CCS cocycle associated with $P$.
Moreover, the restriction 
to the well-configured sequence $ S^{*}_{\rm hem}$ in Example~\ref{i1255},
is smooth by definition.
\end{exa}
\begin{exa}\label{ex23}
Let $G={\rm SL}_n(\C)$ or $G=\SU(n)$, and let $P$ be the polynomial corresponding to the
second Chern class, namely $P(A,B)=\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\mathrm{Tr}(AB)$. 
If $\dim M=3$, obstruction theory implies that every principal $G$-bundle over $M$ is trivial; it is natural to take $\omega_0$ to be the trivial connection.
In addition, we review a known result: 
\begin{thm}\label{tsukau}Let $\lambda$ be $(1/24 \pi ^2)\Tr ( \omega_{\rm CM} \wedge\omega_{\rm CM} \wedge\omega_{\rm CM} )$ as a $G$-invariant $3$-form on $G$,
where $\omega_{\rm CM} \in \AAA^1 (G;\g)$ is the Maurer--Cartan 1-form.
By the $2$-connectivity of $G$, considering the sequence $\{ S_*^{\neq h}\}$ introduced in \eqref{989796}, 
and an appropriate filling $ \sigma$ from Proposition \ref{312}, 
the $3$-cocycle $
 \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\lambda) : G^4 \ra \C/\Z$
is a CCS cocycle $ c_P^{\mathrm{CS}} $. Moreover, if $ G=\SL_2 (\C)$, then $
 \mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\lambda)$ 
is smooth on $S_3^{\neq h} $, and if $G=\SU(2)$, the image of $c_P^{\mathrm{CS}}$ lies in $\R/\Z\subset\C/\Z$.
\end{thm}
The construction is due to some papers \cite{DZ,Dup3,Zic} etc, where deep connections with the
dilogarithm and the extended Bloch group are also developed; we do not recall the details
here.
\end{exa}
\subsection{A lemma on transfer}\label{sec3a4}

In several places we use a basic lemma \ref{321a} below concerning transfer in group cohomology.
For the reader's convenience we include a proof.
Let $\Gamma$ be a group and let $G\subset \Gamma$ be a normal subgroup of finite index $| \Gamma/G| <\infty$.
Let $A$ be either $\R$ or $\R/\Z$, regarded as a trivial $\Gamma$-module.

We review the transfer (corestriction) on homogeneous cochains from \cite[Chapter 4]{Bro}.
Choose a set $T\subset \Gamma$ of representatives for the \emph{right} cosets $G\backslash\Gamma$;
thus $\Gamma=\bigsqcup_{t\in T}Gt$ and we may assume $e\in T$.
For $t\in T$ and $\gamma\in \Gamma$ let $\overline{t\gamma}\in T$ be the unique representative of the right coset $G(t\gamma)$. 
For $\phi \in C^n_{\Delta}(G;A)$ we define a cochain $\Tr(\phi)\in C^n_{\Delta}(\Gamma;A)$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:transfer-def}
\Tr(\phi)(\gamma_0,\ldots,\gamma_n)
:=\sum_{t\in T}\phi\bigl((t\gamma_0) \overline{t\gamma_0}^{-1}, (t\gamma_1 ) \overline{t\gamma_1}^{-1} , \ldots, (t\gamma_n ) \overline{t\gamma_n }^{-1} \bigr).
\end{equation}
Then, the map $\Tr:\ C^*_{\Delta}(G;A)^{G}\longrightarrow C^*_{\Delta}(\Gamma;A)^{\Gamma}$ is known to be 
a chain map, which is the usual transfer (corestriction) for the inclusion $j: G\hookrightarrow  \Gamma$.
Notice that the quotient $\Gamma/G$ acts on $G$ by conjugation,this induces an action of $\Gamma/G$ on $H^*_{\rm gr}(G;A)$.
If a cocycle $\phi$ is invariant under the action, we have $j^* \circ  \Tr([\phi])=|B|\,[\phi]$ by definition.

If $\Gamma$ is a (Fr\'echet) Lie group and $G\subset \Gamma$ is an \emph{open} subgroup of finite index, then each right coset $Gt$ is open and closed.
In this case, for each fixed $t\in T$ the maps $\gamma\mapsto \overline{t\gamma}$ and $\gamma\mapsto t\gamma\,\overline{t\gamma}^{-1}$ are locally smooth on $Gt$,
and \eqref{eq:transfer-def} restricts to chain maps
\[
\Tr:\ C^*_{\rm sm}(G;A)^{G}\to C^*_{\rm sm}(\Gamma;A)^{\Gamma},
\qquad
\Tr:\ C^*_{\rm loc,sm}(G;A)^{G}\to C^*_{\rm loc,sm}(\Gamma;A)^{\Gamma}.
\]

\begin{lem}\label{321a}
Assume that $n$ is odd.
Let $\Gamma$ be a group and let $G\triangleleft \Gamma$ be a normal subgroup of finite index, and set $B:=\Gamma/G$.
Let $\phi\in Z^n_{\Delta}(G;\R/\Z)^{G}$ be a group $n$-cocycle which is invariant under the induced action of $B$.
Set $\widetilde{\phi}:=\Tr(\phi)\in Z^n_{\Delta}(\Gamma;\R/\Z)^{\Gamma}$.

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item The cocycle $\widetilde{\phi}$ satisfies $\widetilde{\phi}|_{G^{n+1}}=|B|\,\phi$, i.e.\ $j^*\widetilde{\phi}=|B|\phi$.
\item Suppose that there exists an integer $c_G\in\N$ with the following property:
      for every $m\in\N$ there exists a group homomorphism
      $\iota_m : \Z/m \to G$ such that the map
      \[
        H_n^{\rm gr}(\Z/m; \Z) \longrightarrow \Q/\Z,
        \qquad
        \kappa \longmapsto \langle \iota_m^* [\phi], \kappa \rangle
      \]
      has image
      $\{ [c_G s/m] \in \Q/\Z \mid s \in \Z\}$.
      Then $H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma)$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $\Q/\Z$.
\item Let $q:\Gamma\to G'$ be a surjective homomorphism whose kernel $K:=\Ker(q)$ is finite and central.
      Then there exists a class $[\phi']\in H^n_{\rm gr}(G';\R/\Z)$ such that
      \[
      q^*[\phi']=|K|\,[\widetilde{\phi}]\in H^n_{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\R/\Z).
      \]
      Moreover, if the hypothesis in \textup{(ii)} holds for $\phi$, then $H_n(G')$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $\Q/\Z$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lem}
\begin{proof}
\noindent\textbf{(i)} This is explained above.

\noindent\textbf{(ii)}
Let ${\rm ev}:=\langle[\widetilde{\phi}],-\rangle:\Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)\to \Tor(\R/\Z)=\Q/\Z$.
For each $m$ let $\tau_m\in H_n^{\rm gr}(\Z/m;\Z)\cong\Z/m$ be a generator, set
$\bar\iota_m:=j\circ\iota_m$, and put $x_m:=\bar\iota_{m*}(\tau_m)\in \Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)$.
Naturality and \textup{(i)} give
\[{
\rm ev}(x_m)=\langle \bar\iota_m^{\,*}[\widetilde{\phi}],\tau_m\rangle
=\langle \iota_m^{\,*}(j^*[\widetilde{\phi}]),\tau_m\rangle
=|B|\langle \iota_m^{\,*}[\phi],\tau_m\rangle \in \Q/\Z.
\]
Hence $\Im({\rm ev})$ contains $\{[|B|c_G s/m]\mid s\in\Z\}$ for every $m$.
Since multiplication by $|B|c_G$ is surjective on $\Q/\Z$, we get $\Im({ \rm ev})=\Q/\Z$.
Thus $\Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)\twoheadrightarrow\Q/\Z$; as $\Q/\Z$ is divisible (hence injective),
this surjection splits and $\Q/\Z$ embeds into $H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma)$.

\noindent\textbf{(iii)}
Since $K$ is finite, $H^q_{\rm gr}(K;\R/\Z)$ is $|K|$-torsion for $q>0$.
Hence the inflation map $q^*:H^n_{\rm gr} (G';\R/\Z)\to H^n_{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\R/\Z)$ has cokernel annihilated by $|K|$
(e.g.\ by the Lyndon--Hochschild--Serre spectral sequence).
Therefore $|K|[\widetilde{\phi}]\in \mathrm{Im}(q^*)$, so we can choose $[\phi']\in H^n_{\rm gr}(G';\R/\Z)$ with
$q^*[\phi']=|K|\,[\widetilde{\phi}]$.

Assume moreover the hypothesis in \textup{(ii)}.
Set $\mathrm{ev}_{\Gamma}:=\langle[\widetilde{\phi}],-\rangle:\Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)\to\Q/\Z$
and $\mathrm{ev}_{G'}:=\langle[\phi'],-\rangle:\Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(G';\Z)\to\Q/\Z$.
Then for any $x\in \Tor H_n^{\rm gr}(\Gamma;\Z)$ we have
\[
\mathrm{ev}_{G'}(q_*x)=\langle[\phi'],q_*x\rangle=\langle q^*[\phi'],x\rangle
=|K|\langle[\widetilde{\phi}],x\rangle=|K|\mathrm{ev}_{\Gamma}(x).
\]
By \textup{(ii)} the map $\mathrm{ev}_{\Gamma}$ is surjective, and multiplication by $|K|$ is surjective on $\Q/\Z$,
hence $\mathrm{ev}_{G'}$ is surjective.
Since $\Q/\Z$ is divisible, the surjection $\Tor H_n(G';\Z)\twoheadrightarrow \Q/\Z$ splits, and therefore
$\Q/\Z$ embeds into $H_n^{\rm gr}(G')$.
\end{proof}

\[

\begin{thm}\label{main4}
Let $\alpha_{\rm st}\in{\cal A}^1(S^3)$ be the standard contact 1-form on the $3$-sphere $S^3$
(defining the standard contact structure $\ker(\alpha_{\rm st})$).
Then $H_3^{\rm gr}\bigl(\Diff_{\alpha_{\rm st}}(S^3)\bigr)$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to ${\Bbb Q}/{\Bbb Z}$.
\end{thm}

\noindent\textbf{Ideas of the proof.}
Compared with much of the existing literature on degree-three classes for diffeomorphism groups,
our results are formulated at the (locally) cocycle level. In fact, 
The key step is the construction of a nontrivial locally smooth ${\Bbb R}/{\Bbb Z}$-valued group $3$-cocycle
of Chern--Simons type \cite{CS}.
Starting from an invariant differential form $\lambda$ on a (Fr\'echet) Lie group ${\cal G}$,
we construct a cochain by integrating $\lambda$ over a family of simplices with prescribed vertices
(Section~\ref{sec33233}).
In infinite dimensions such a straightening is not available canonically on the full Cartesian power
${\cal G}^{n+1}$, and even in finite dimensions one typically obtains smoothness only on suitable open subsets.
To organize this systematically, we work in the restriction-of-domain framework of Definition~\ref{asfa}:
we replace the full homogeneous complex by an invariant subcomplex ${\Bbb Z}\langle S_*\rangle$
coming from a \emph{well-configured} sequence ${\cal S}=\{S_n\subset {\cal G}^{n+1}\}$
(Section~\ref{sec2d991}).

For the diffeomorphism groups considered here, we take $S_n$ to be the set of \emph{$U$-small tuples}
$(g_0,\dots,g_n)$ for which all relative differences $g_i^{-1}g_j$ lie in a fixed identity neighbourhood $U$
(Definition~\eqref{def:U-small}).
A fixed convex chart around the identity then yields an explicit \emph{affine straightening}:
using an ``affine join'' inside the chart we construct a filling $\sigma$ over $\Ss_{{\cal G},U}$
(Subsection~\ref{sec223344}) and hence a cochain $\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\lambda): {\cal G}^{n+1} \rightarrow {\Bbb R}/{\Bbb Z}$ by integration.
To obtain an honest ${\Bbb R}/{\Bbb Z}$-valued cocycle, one must control periods and, crucially, eliminate the
low-degree homotopy obstruction encoded in Proposition~\ref{baas} (notably involving $\pi_2({\cal G} )$).
In the groups in the theorems, this obstruction can be verified to vanish using concrete homotopy-type results:
in the $3$-manifold cases we use Smale-type theorems identifying
$\Diff_v (M)$ with the isometry group $\mathrm{Isom}^+(M)$---namely the generalized Smale conjecture proved by Bamler--Kleiner
for spherical space forms \cite{BK}, and Gabai's theorem in the hyperbolic case \cite{Gabai}.
Finally, Proposition~\ref{43333} shows that the derivation of the cocycle $\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\lambda)$ 
is a representative cocycle in the
Gel'fand--Fuks cohomology of the Lie algebra of $\Diff_\lambda (M) $.
This compatibility is the main tool for detecting nontriviality by restriction to compact subgroups and
comparison with classical Cheeger--Chern--Simons classes (see Section \ref{sec2233} and ~\ref{sssdd} or \cite{DPS,DZ}).

This idea yields new and computable $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$-torsion phenomena in $H^{\mathrm{gr}}_{3}$
for several classical diffeomorphism groups arising in low-dimensional and symplectic-contact topology.
In fact, for symplectic manifolds, we use known homotopy equivalences for ${\Bbb C} P^1$ and the results of Gromov
for ${\Bbb C} P^2$ \cite{Gro} and Abreu--McDuff for $({\Bbb C} P^1\times{\Bbb C} P^1,\omega_1\oplus\omega_1)$ \cite{AM},
which again imply the required vanishing of $\pi_2$ in the identity component; 
Theorems \ref{main3}--\ref{main4} follow by applying the ideas presented above.
Incidentally, the hyperbolic case (Section~\ref{hyp11}) yields a related ${\Bbb R}$-valued $3$-cocycle whose
vanishing in cohomology remains open.

\noindent\textbf{Organization of the paper.}
Section~\ref{sec299} fixes conventions on (locally smooth) group (co)homology,
the restriction-of-domain method, and well-configured complexes.
Section~\ref{sec33233} adapts Dupont's straightening framework \cite{Dup1,Dup2,Dup3} to well-configured complexes.
Section~\ref{sec2233} reviews Cheeger--Chern--Simons theory and proves Theorem~\ref{main1};
the hyperbolic case is discussed in Section~\ref{hyp11}.
Section~\ref{sec32884} treats symplectic manifolds and proves Theorem~\ref{main3}.
Finally, Section~\ref{sec32d} deals with contact manifolds and proves Theorem~\ref{main4}.

\noindent\textbf{Conventions.}
Throughout, ${\cal G}$ denotes a topological group with identity element $e$.
Unless stated otherwise, manifolds are connected, closed, oriented, and smooth.

To get an honest cocycle, one must “control periods and, crucially, eliminate the low-degree homotopy obstruction encoded in Proposition~\ref{baas} (notably involving $\pi_2({\cal G})$)”; in the groups of interest this obstruction is shown to vanish using “concrete homotopy-type results”, e.g. in the $3$-manifold cases using Smale-type theorems identifying $\Diff_v(M)$ with $\mathrm{Isom}^+(M)$ (Bamler--Kleiner for spherical space forms, and Gabai in the hyperbolic case). Finally, Proposition~\ref{43333} identifies the derivation of $\mathcal{F}_{\sigma}(\lambda)$ with a cocycle in Gel'fand--Fuks cohomology of the Lie algebra of $\Diff_\lambda(M)$; this “compatibility is the main tool for detecting nontriviality by restriction to compact subgroups and comparison with classical Cheeger--Chern--Simons classes”.

    For all $b\geq 2$, there exists infinitely many square-free palindromes in base $b$.

mcq.question: Let $b$ be an integer with $b\ge 2$. A positive integer $n$ is called a palindrome in base $b$ if its base-$b$ expansion reads the same forwards and backwards, and it is called square-free if it is not divisible by the square of any integer $>1$. Under these assumptions on $b$, which statement correctly asserts an existence result for such integers $n$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: For every integer $b\ge 2$, there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ that are palindromes in base $b$ and are square-free.

choices.label: B
choices.text:
For every integer $b\ge 2$, there exists an $x_0(b)$ such that for all $x\ge x_0(b)$ one has
\[
\#\{n\in \msP_b^*(x): n\ \text{is square-free}\}
=\frac{\#\msP_b^*(x)}{\zeta(2)}\prod_{p\mid b^2-b}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^2}\right)^{-1}\left(1+O_b\left(\frac{1}{(\log x)^2}\right)\right).
\]
In particular, there are infinitely many square-free palindromes in base $b$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There exist infinitely many integers $b\ge 2$ for which there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ that are palindromes in base $b$ and are square-free.

choices.label: D
choices.text:
For every integer $b\ge 2$, there exists a constant $c>0$ (independent of $b$) such that for all sufficiently large $x$,
\[
\#\{n\in \msP_b^*(x): n\ \text{is square-free}\}\ge c\,\#\msP_b^*(x).
\]
In particular, for every $b\ge 2$ there are infinitely many square-free palindromes in base $b$.

choices.label: E
choices.text:
For every integer $b\ge 2$, for any $\varepsilon>0$, and uniformly for all $x^{1/4}\le D\le x^{2/5}$, the number $S_b(x,D)$ of base-$b$ palindromes $n\le x$ divisible by some square $d^2\ge D$ satisfies
\[
S_b(x,D)\ll_{b,\varepsilon}\frac{x^{1/2+\varepsilon}}{D^{1/2}}.
\]
Consequently, for every $b\ge 2$ there are infinitely many square-free palindromes in base $b$.

post_theorem_intro_text:
Originally E.M. Landesman and A.C. Lazer \cite{L} assumed additionally that the eigenvalue $\lambda _k$ is simple. Soon, S.A. Williams \cite{wi} produced the more general statement given above. However,  for a while no examples for multiple eigenvalues were known, until we observed in \cite{K} that another classical result of A.C. Lazer and D.E. Leach \cite{L1} on periodic solutions of semilinear harmonic oscillator  provides an example to  Theorem \ref{thm:1} in case of double eigenvalues (giving incidentally another proof of  Lazer-Leach theorem, in addition to a number of other known proofs, see e.g., \cite{H} and \cite{K}).
We showed in \cite{K} that while the necessary condition of Lazer-Leach result is easy to prove, the sufficiency part follows by verifying  the condition (\ref{2}), and applying Theorem \ref{thm:1}.
\medskip

In this paper we prove a similar result for a  disc in $R^2$, thus providing the first PDE example for Theorem \ref{thm:1} in case of a multiple dimensional eigenspace.  Even for simple domains the eigenspace of a multiple eigenvalue can be very complicated, and multiplicity of eigenvalues may vary in non-obvious ways. So that verifying the inequality (\ref{2}) for any element $w(x)$ of the eigenspace appears to be very challenging for other domains (the integrals $\int _{w>0} w(x) \, dx$ and $\int _{w<0} w(x) \, dx$ are unlikely to remain constant over an eigenspace).
\medskip

\noindent
{\large \bf Example }  Let $D=(0,\pi) \times (0,\pi)$ in $R^2$. The eigenvalues of 
\[
\Delta u +\lambda u=0 \,, \; \; \mbox{in $D$}\, \; \; u=0 \; \; \mbox{on $\partial D$}
\]
are $\lambda _{nm}=n^2+m^2$ with positive integers $n$ and $m$, corresponding to the eigenfunctions $\sin nx \sin my$, see e.g., \cite{pr}. These eigenfunctions are obtained by separation of variables, and there are no other eigenfunctions since these eigenfunctions form a complete set in $L^2(D)$.   The principal eigenvalue $\lambda _1=2$ is simple, with the corresponding eigenfunction $\sin x \sin y>0$. The eigenvalue $\lambda _2=5=1^2+2^2$ has multiplicity two, with
the eigenspace spanned by $\sin x \sin 2y, \sin 2x \sin y$. The eigenvalue $\lambda _3=8=2^2+2^2$ is simple, with
the eigenspace spanned by $\sin 2x \sin 2y$. The eigenvalue $50=1^2+7^2=5^2+5^2$ is triple, with
the eigenspace spanned by $\sin x \sin 7y, \sin 7x \sin y, \sin 5x \sin 5y$. The eigenvalue $65=1^2+8^2=4^2+7^2$ is quadruple,  the eigenvalue $325=1^2+18^2=6^2+17^2=10^2+15^2$ has multiplicity six, and so on. It is natural to ask if there is an eigenvalue of any multiplicity. In number theoretic terms the possible conjecture is: for any even integer $2m$ one can find an integer $N$ that can be represented as $N=p^2+q^2$, with integers $p \ne q$, in exactly $m$ different ways, while  for any odd integer $2m+1$ one can find an integer $M$ that can be represented as $M=p^2+q^2$, with integers $p \ne q$, in exactly $m$ different ways, and in addition, $M=r^2+r^2$ for some integer $r>0$.
\medskip

By contrast, for a disc $B _a: x^2+y^2 <a^2$ in $R^2$, we show that all eigenvalues of the Laplacian have multiplicity two, except for the principal one (which is simple), and that the integrals $\int _{w>0} w(x,y) \, dxdy$ and $\int _{w<0} w(x,y) \, dxdy$ remain constant over the entire eigenspaces, and can be explicitly calculated. We present a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of solutions of the problem (\ref{0}) on $B _a$, for this case of resonance at a double eigenvalue. We prove the necessity part directly, while sufficiency is derived by verifying the conditions of Theorem \ref{thm:1}. Our result can be seen as a PDE analog of the Lazer-Leach theorem. As an application, we give a condition for unboundness of all solutions of the corresponding semilinear heat equation.
\medskip

Radial solutions on balls in $R^n$ were studied extensively, see e.g., P. Korman \cite{K2} or T. Ouyang and J. Shi \cite{OS}, stimulated by  the classical theorem of B. Gidas, W.-M. Ni and L. Nirenberg \cite{GNN} which asserts that any positive solution of semilinear Dirichlet problem on a ball is necessarily radially symmetric. Our result suggests that ball may be a special domain even when studying sign-changing non-symmetric solutions.
\medskip

Previously, P. Korman and D.S. Schmidt \cite{ks} studied resonance at the principal eigenvalue on $B$. They constructed $g(u)$ for which the problem has infinitely many solutions {\em for any} $f(x,y) \in L^2(B _a)$.

post_theorem_intro_text:
\paragraph{\textbf{On the method of proof}}

Comparing our proof for $n>2$ with the proof given in \cite{jiangliu} for $n=2$, the key difference lies in the strategies used to classify non-amenable invariant subfactors, which is also the hard core for the whole proof.

In \cite{jiangliu}, the classification (for non-amenable invariant subalgebras) directly follows from   \cite[Theorem 5.1]{cds} since $G_2$ is an icc exact group which satisfies condition 2) in \cite[Theorem 5.1]{cds}. We remark that the proof of this theorem is largely based on techniques developed within Popa's powerful deformation/rigidity theory framework. It is not a surprise that this strategy is not applicable to $G_n$ for $n>2$.  Indeed, Chifan-Sinclair \cite[Theorem A]{cs} proved that if a group $G$ satisfies this condition, then $L(G)$ is solid in the sense of Ozawa \cite{ozawa_solid}, i.e. $A'\cap L(G)$ is amenable for every diffuse von Neumann subalgebra $A\subset L(G)$. It is clear that for $n>2$, if we take $A=L(\mathbb{Z})\subset L(\mathbb{Z}^n)\subset L(G_n)$, where $\mathbb{Z}=\langle e_1\rangle$ with $e_1=(1,0,\ldots, 0)^t\in \mathbb{Z}^n$, then $L(SL_2(\mathbb{Z}))\subset A'\cap L(G_n)$. Thus $L(G_n)$ is not solid.

To handle the abovementioned issue, we apply the character approach developed in \cites{jz,dj} while studying the ISR property. The new ingredient is Lemma \ref{3.2}, where we proved that $\mathbb{Z}^n$ satisfies a modified version of the so-called non-factorizable regular character property as introduced in \cite{dj}.

In fact, the above approach also works uniformly for all $n\geq 2$ (see Proposition \ref{prop: classify_invariant_subfactors}), although we need to split the whole proof according to the parity of $n$ due to the existence of non-trivial centers in $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ for even $n$. Even for $n=2$, this yields an alternative proof for the main theorem in the previous work \cite{jiangliu}. Indeed, instead of splitting the proof by considering amenable/non-amenable invariant subalgebras $P$ as in \cite{jiangliu}, we now proceed by first classifying the center $\mathcal{Z}(P)$ (see Lemma \ref{3.5}).

Finally, we note that although our proof makes no direct appeal to the property (T) of $G_n (n>2)$ or the relative property (T) for the pair $(G_2, \mathbb{Z}^2)$, the rigidity phenomena for the action $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})\curvearrowright \mathbb{T}^n$ that we do use, in particular, the classification of its ergodic measures \cite[Proposition 9]{burger} and of its factor actions \cite[Example 5.9]{wit}, are themselves indirect manifestations of rigidity for the ambient group or relative rigidity for the group-subgroup pair. Thus property (T) for $G_n (n>2)$ or the relative property (T) for the pair $(G_2, \mathbb{Z}^2)$ implicitly underpins our results. \\

\paragraph{\textbf{Organization of the paper}} The detailed plan of the article is as follows: after this introduction, in Section 2 we prepare lemmas on group aspects and dynamical properties related to $G_n$, and prove the non-factorizable property for $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$-invariant characters on $\mathbb{Z}^n$ (Lemma \ref{3.2}). Besides the proof of Corollary \ref{cor}, the proof of Theorem \ref{thm} takes up the whole section 3. \\

The work is partially supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 12471118).

theorem.content:
Let $G$ be a compact, simple and simply connecetd Lie group, and let $\alpha \in {\rm H}^3_G(G,\mathbb{Z})$ be the canonical generator. There exists an 
$\mathbb{S}^1$-central extension of Lie groupoids representing an 
$\mathbb{S}^1$-gerbe over the differentiable stack 
$[G/G]$, whose Dixmier-Douady class is $\alpha$.

sketch:
The post-theorem introduction explains that the result ("Theorem A") is proved using "symplectic reduction and the theory of symplectic groupoids." One starts from the Kac–Moody $\mathbb{S}^1$-central extension $\widetilde{LG}\to LG$ and considers the trivialized cotangent bundle of $\widetilde{LG}$, which "naturally carries both a symplectic groupoid structure and a Hamiltonian $\mathbb{S}^1$-action." Then one performs "symplectic reduction at a nontrivial regular value of the moment map," obtaining a "reduced symplectic groupoid with underlying space $LG\times L\mathfrak{g}^*$." The "moment level set, together with this reduced groupoid, provide the desired $\mathbb{S}^1$-central extension," and "the reduced symplectic form plays the role of the curvature data for the associated gerbe."

To identify the Dixmier–Douady class, the reduced symplectic groupoid $LG\times L\mathfrak{g}^*\rightrightarrows L\mathfrak{g}^*$ is related to the AMM quasi-symplectic groupoid $G\times G \rightrightarrows G$ by using "the theory of $q$-Hamiltonian spaces" to construct "a Morita equivalence between these two groupoids" and to connect "the reduced symplectic form with the AMM cocycle $\omega_D+\Omega$." This "comparison implies that the gerbe obtained from symplectic reduction represents precisely the class $\alpha$."

ref_dict.thm:almosteverywhere:
\begin{thm}\label{thm:almosteverywhere}
Let $G$ be  a second-countable locally compact  abelian group acting continuously on a second-countable locally compact  space $X$. Suppose  $\m \in \ProbG(X)$ and  $\rho \in \Prob(\Erg(X))$ satisfy 
\[
\int_X f(x) \, \dd \m(x) = \int_{\Erg(X)} \int_X f(y) \, \dd \omega(y) \, \dd \rho(\omega) \qquad \forall f \in \Cz(X) \,.
\]
If $B \subset \widehat G$ is a Borel set such that $P_\m(B) = \id_{L^2(X,\m)}$, then  $P_\omega(B) = \id_{L^2(X,\omega)}$  for $\rho$-a.e. $\omega \in \Erg(X)$. 
\end{thm}

post_theorem_intro_text:
It is the goal of the paper to show that the answer is yes. 

Our approach is as follows: starting with a mean almost periodic measure $\mu$ on $G$, we can construct a $G$-invariant probability measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the hull $\mathbb{X}(\mu)$  with pure point spectrum \cite{LSS,LSS2}. If we can prove that at least one ergodic measure $\omega$ on $\mathbb{X}(\mu)$ has pure point spectrum, we can deduce that $\mathbb{X}(\mu)$ admits Besicovitch almost periodic measures, from which the claim follows.

To this end, we prove a much more general result about $G$-invariant probability measures on topological dynamical systems. Indeed, let $(X,G)$ be a topological dynamical system with $X$ and $G$ locally compact and second-countable, and let $\mathsf{m}$ be a $G$-invariant probability measure on $X$. Let $\rho$ be the measure on $\operatorname{Erg}(X)$ which represents $\mathsf{m}$ via the Choquet theorem. In our main result (Theorem~\ref{thm:almosteverywhere}) we show that if $B \subseteq \widehat{G}$ is a Borel set such that the spectrum of $\mathsf{m}$ is contained in $B$, then for $\rho$-a.s. all $\omega \in \operatorname{Erg}(X)$, the spectrum of $\omega$ is also contained in $B$. As a consequence we get that if $\mathsf{m}$ has pure point spectrum, then so does $\omega \in \operatorname{Erg}(X)$ for $\rho$-a.s. $\omega$.

For brevity, we require that  all our compact and locally compact spaces/groups be Hausdorff by definition.

The paper is organized as follows: In Section~\ref{sect:prel} we review some basic definitions and properties of functions and measures. We continue in Section~\ref{sect:Borel} by reviewing properties of the Borel structure on the set of probability measures on a second-countable locally compact Hausdorff space $X$. In Section~\ref{sec:choquet} we briefly review Choquet theory, while in Section~\ref{sect:spectral} we review spectral measures and spectral decomposition. Given a dynamical system $(X,G)$ and a $G$-invariant probability measure $\mathsf{m}$ on $X$, Choquet theory tells us that there exists a probability measure $\rho$ on $\operatorname{Erg}(X)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-rep}
\int_X f(x) \, \mbox{\rm d} \mathsf{m}(x) = \int_{\operatorname{Erg}(X)} \int_X f(y) \, \mbox{\rm d} \omega(y) \, \mbox{\rm d} \rho(\omega) \qquad \forall f \in C^{}_{0}(X) \,.
\end{equation}
We show in Section~\ref{sect:main} that \eqref{eq-rep} holds for all $f \in B(X)$, the algebra of bounded Borel functions. As a consequence, we get in Theorem~\ref{thm:almosteverywhere} that if the spectrum of $L^2(X,\mathsf{m})$ is supported inside some Borel set $B\subseteq \widehat{G}$ then so is the spectrum of $L^2(X,\omega)$ for $\rho$-almost all $\omega \in \operatorname{Erg}(X)$.

As immediate consequences, we get that if $L^2(X,\mathsf{m})$ has pure point or singular spectrum, then so does $L^2(X, \omega)$ for $\rho$-almost all $\omega \in \operatorname{Erg}(X)$. We conclude the paper by showing in Section~\ref{sec:Bap} that if $\mu \in \mathcal{M}^\infty(G)$ is mean almost periodic with respect to some van Hove sequence $\mathcal{A}$ then $\mu$ is Besicovitch almost periodic with respect to some translated subsequence of $\mathcal{A}$.

Finally, applying this to $\mathsf{m}$ on $\mathbb{X}(\mu)$ and using that $\mu$ is mean almost periodic (with respect to some van Hove sequence $\mathcal{A}$), the paper concludes (Section~\ref{sec:Bap}) that $\mu$ is Besicovitch almost periodic with respect to some translated subsequence of $\mathcal{A}$ (i.e. one can choose a suitable averaging sequence $\mathcal{B}$).

theorem.content:
\label{cor}
Let $G=\mathbb{Z}^2\rtimes SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$. Then $L(\mathbb{Z}^2\rtimes \{\pm I_2\})$ is the unique maximal Haagerup $G$-invariant von Neumann subalgebra in $L(G)$, where $I_2$ denotes the identity matrix in $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
theorem.label: cor

post_theorem_intro_text:
Next, let us comment on the proof of Theorem \ref{thm}.
For the proof, we combine \cite[Theorem 5.1]{cds} with \cite[Theorem A]{aho} to  reduce the study to the case $P\subseteq L(\mathbb{Z}^2\rtimes \{\pm I_2\})$. Then by applying techniques as introduced in \cite{aj}, a considerable amount of effort has to be devoted to showing that $P$ actually lies in $L(\mathbb{Z}^2)$ unless $P=L(d\mathbb{Z}^2\rtimes \{\pm I_2\})$, where $d\in\{1, 2\}$.
We remark that a similar strategy can also be applied to the wreath product group $\mathbb{Z}\wr F_2$, see Section \ref{section: last remark}.

This paper is organized as follows: after recalling  relevant techniques in Section \ref{section: preliminaries}, we present the proof of Theorem \ref{thm} and Corollary \ref{cor} in Section \ref{section: proof}. Finally, in Section \ref{section: last remark}, we collect some remarks and open questions related to this work. 

In this paper, we usually use $\tau$ to mean a trace on a finite von Neumann algebra, e.g., a crossed product or group von Neumann algebra, which will be clear from the context.
\medskip

\paragraph{\textbf{Acknowledgements}} 

This work is partially supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 12001081, No. 12271074) and the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities (Grant No. DUT19RC(3)075). Part of this work was done during the visiting of Y. J. to the Institute for Advances Study in Mathematics of HIT in October, 2023. Y. J. is grateful to Prof. Simeng Wang for his invitation and hospitality during this visiting and to Prof. Adam Skalski and Dr. Amrutam Tattwamasi for helpful discussions on this paper.

theorem.content:
\label{th:main}
Let $n \geq 3$. If $\pi_{n+k}({\mathcal N}) \neq \{0\}$ for some $k \geq 0$, then there exists a nontrivial, $C^{1,\alpha}$-regular $n$-harmonic map from ${\mathbb S}^n$ into ${\mathcal N}$, where $\alpha$ is a small positive number.
theorem.label: th:main

ref_dict.s:main:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:estimateonlittlef}
\|f\|_{L^{\frac{n+\sigma}{p}}(B(0,20))}
\aleq
\|\nabla u\|_{L^{n+\sigma}(B(0,20))}^{p}
\aleq_\Lambda 1.
\end{equation}
Let $s_0>0$ be given by \Cref{th:anna}. Shrinking $s_0$ if necessary, we may assume that
\[
0<s\le s_0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
s<\frac{n\sigma}{2n+\sigma}.
\]
Fix such an $s$. Then, for all $p\in[n,p_1]$,
\[
\frac{n}{n-s}\le \frac{2n+\sigma}{2n},
\qquad \text{and} \qquad 
\frac{np'}{n+(1-s)p'}\le \frac{2n+\sigma}{2n} < \frac{n+\sigma}{p}.
\]
Moreover, by possibly shrinking $p_1$ once more so that $p_1<\frac{n}{1-s}$, we ensure that
\[
\frac{np'}{n+(1-s)p'}>1
\qquad\text{for all } p\in[n,p_1].
\]
Hence, we first apply \eqref{eq:Annainequality}, then H\"{o}lder inequality, and finally \eqref{eq:estimateonlittlef}, which yields
\[
\bigl[\,|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u\,\bigr]_{W^{s,p'}(B(0,15))}
\aleq_\Lambda
\|f\|_{L^{\frac{n+\sigma}{p}}(B(0,30))}+1
\aleq_\Lambda 1.
\]
Moreover, the following inequality holds for $p \geq 2$ (see for instance \cite[Lemma 2.3.7]{M})
\[
 \abs{|\nabla u|^{p-2}(x) \nabla u(x)-|\nabla u|^{p-2}(y) \nabla u(y)} \ageq_{p} \abs{\nabla u(x)-\nabla u(y)}^{p-1}.
\]
We find that
\[
 \int_{B(0,15)}\int_{B(0,15)} \frac{\abs{\nabla u(x)- \nabla u(y)}^{p}}{|x-y|^{n+\frac{s}{2(p-1)} p}}\, dx\, dy \aleq_{\Lambda}1. 
\]
Setting $t_0 = \frac{s}{2(p_1-1)} \leq \frac{s}{2(p-1)}$ we conclude.
\end{proof}

\section{Conclusion: Proof of Theorem~\ref{th:main}}\label{s:main}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \Cref{th:main}]
Let $p_0=n+1$ and let us take $\eps$ from \Cref{th:epsreg}. Recall that we assume that $k \geq 1$ (because  $k=0$ is known already). That is, we can apply \Cref{co:minmaxpharmmaps} to find a sequence $p_j \xrightarrow{j \to \infty} n^+$ and a sequence of nontrivial $p_j$-harmonic maps $u_{p_j} \in C^{1,\alpha_j}(\S^n,\n)$. There are two possible cases.

\textsc{Case 1:} \underline{There are no bubbles}, i.e., for all $x \in \S^n$ there exists $\rho_x > 0$ such that
 \[
  \limsup_{j \to \infty} \int_{B(x,\rho_x)} |\nabla u_{p_j}|^{n} < \eps^n.
 \]
In this case we cover the compact set $\S^n$ by finitely many balls $B(x,\rho_x/2)$, apply \Cref{th:epsreg} on each $B(x,\rho_x/2)$,  and from the embedding $W^{t_0,p_j}_{loc} \hookrightarrow W^{\frac{t_0}{2},n}_{loc}$ obtain\footnote{For $s\in(0,1)$ in general there is \emph{no} embedding 
$W^{s,p}_{\loc}\hookrightarrow W^{s,q}_{\loc}$ when $p>q$; see \cite{Mironescu-Sickel}.}
\[
 \sup_j [\nabla u_{p_j}]_{ W^{\frac{t_0}{2},n}(\S^n)} < \infty.
\]
Thus, up to a subsequence, 
\[
 u_{p_j} \to u \quad \text {strongly in } W^{1,n+\sigma} \text{ for some $\sigma > 0$.}
\]
By Vitali's convergence theorem we then have 
\[
 \int_{\S^n} |\nabla u|^n = \lim_{j \to \infty} \int_{\S^n} |\nabla u_{p_j}|^{p_j} >0.
\]
By the strong convergence, we can also pass to the limit in the equation \eqref{eq:pharmonic} and conclude that $u$ is an $n$-harmonic map. The map $u$ cannot be trivial since $\|\nabla u\|_{L^n} > 0$. Since $u \in W^{1,n+\gamma}$ we know that $u$ is H\"{o}lder continuous. Thus, as in \cite[Section 3]{HLp}, $u \in C^{1,\alpha}$ is a nontrivial $n$-harmonic map.

\textsc{Case 2}: \underline{There is an isolated bubble}, i.e.,

Throughout the paper we assume $n\ge3$. The two-dimensional case can be treated by the same arguments with minor modifications; since the corresponding results for harmonic maps are already well known (see \cite{Lamm06} and references therein), we do not include them here.

The existence result in this theorem is in line with general expectations in the theory of harmonic maps. In the case $k=0$, that is, when $\pi_{n}({\mathcal N}) \neq \{0\}$, it follows from the classical Sacks--Uhlenbeck theory \cite{SacksU81}, since $\pi_{n}({\mathcal N})$ is generated by homotopy classes for which the $n$-energy admits a minimizer. The corresponding result for the $n$-harmonic maps was proved by \cite{Nakauchi-Takakuwa,Kawai-Nakauchi-Takeuchi}. See also \cite{Mazowiecka-Schikorra23} for related minimization results in a fractional framework.

When $\pi_{n}({\mathcal N})= \{0\}$ but $\pi_{n+k}({\mathcal N}) \ni \alpha \neq 0$, one is naturally lead to seek critical points of the $n$-energy via a $\min$-$\max$ construction of the form
\[
 \inf_{\Phi \in \alpha}\ \max_{t\in [-1,1]^k}\ \mathcal{E}_n\big( \Phi(\cdot,t) \big).
\]
This is the equivalent approach to Birkhoff's min-max construction of nontrivial closed geodesics on manifolds diffeomorphic to the sphere ${\mathbb S}^2$. A direct implementation of this strategy at the critical exponent $n$ is, however, obstructed by the failure of the Palais--Smale condition in $W^{1,n}$.

In the recent work \cite{DML25}, this difficulty is overcome by developing a refined analytical framework, leading to a proof of the theorem \Cref{th:main} in dimension $n=3$, and in dimensions $n\geq 4$ in the case of manifolds which are spheres or Lie groups. The present work provides an alternative approach, which applies to all dimensions $n\ge3$ and to arbitrary smooth closed target manifolds ${\mathcal N}$.

The starting point is classical. For $p > n$, we consider the perturbed energy
\[
 \mathcal{E}_p(u) \coloneqq \int_{{\mathbb S}^n} |\nabla u|^p, \quad  u\colon {\mathbb S}^n \to {\mathcal N}.
\]
For $p>n$, the functional satisfies the Palais--Smale condition, allowing one to construct non-trivial critical points of the associated Euler--Lagrange equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pharmonic}
 -{\rm div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2} \nabla u) = |\nabla u|^{p-2} A(u)[\nabla u,\nabla u].
\end{equation}
These are obtained through the min-max scheme
\[
 \beta_p \coloneqq \min_{\Phi \in \alpha}\ \max_{ t\in [-1,1]^k}\ \mathcal{E}_p \big(\Phi(\cdot,t) \big).
\]
Provided that $\liminf_{p \to n} \beta_p > 0$, \Cref{th:main} follows  from a one-bubble compactness result: for any sequence $p \to n^+$, $p>n$ and any corresponding sequence of $p$-harmonic maps $u_p \in W^{1,p}({\mathbb S}^n,{\mathcal N})$, one of the following holds, up to a subsequence. Either $u_p$ converges strongly in $W^{1,n+\sigma}$  for some $\sigma > 0$, meaning that the limit is a nontrivial $n$-harmonic map; or there exists at least one nontrivial bubble, which, after rescaling, is a nontrivial $n$-harmonic map.

{\bf Outline.} Since the case $k=0$ is known (see for instance \cite{W1986,W1988} or \cite[Theorem 0]{Kawai-Nakauchi-Takeuchi}), we focus on the case $k \geq 1$. That is, throughout the remainder of this article we assume $\pi_{n+k}(\mathcal{N})\neq \{0\}$. In \Cref{s:prelim} we establish the validity of the min-max construction for $p$-harmonic maps and $p > n$. \Cref{s:epsreg} explains the main analytical tool of the paper. There we prove an $\varepsilon$-regularity result for $p$-harmonic maps under a uniform $p$-energy bound. Instead of deriving higher \emph{second-order} regularity, we obtain a fractional gain in the differentiability, showing that solutions belong locally to $W^{1+\delta, p}$ for some $\delta>0$. This fractional improvement is sufficient to ensure the compactness needed in the bubbling analysis. The argument relies on the contemporary regularity theory for the $p$-Laplacian combined with the classical stability estimate in the spirit of Iwaniec--Sbordone \cite{Iwaniec-Sbordone}, which provides a uniform control of the $(n+\sigma)$-energy for some $\sigma>0$.

Finally, in \Cref{s:main} we combine the previous results to prove the main theorem. Using the compactness provided by the fractional regularity improvement and a one-bubble extraction argument, we show the existence of a nontrivial $n$-harmonic map.

\label{th:main}
Let $n \geq 3$. If $\pi_{n+k}({\mathcal N}) \neq \{0\}$ for some $k \geq 0$, then there exists a nontrivial, $C^{1,\alpha}$-regular $n$-harmonic map from ${\mathbb S}^n$ into ${\mathcal N}$, where $\alpha$ is a small positive number.

mcq.question: Let $n\ge 3$, and let $\mathcal N$ be a space such that for some integer $k\ge 0$ one has $\pi_{n+k}(\mathcal N)\neq\{0\}$. Under these assumptions, which statement asserts the existence of an object satisfying the strongest conclusion justified by the hypotheses?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists a nontrivial (i.e., not constant) $C^{1,\alpha}$-regular $n$-harmonic map $u:\mathbb S^n\to\mathcal N$ for some small positive number $\alpha>0$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There exists a nontrivial (i.e., not constant) $C^{1,\alpha}$-regular $n$-harmonic map $u:\mathbb S^n\to\mathcal N$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There exists a nontrivial (i.e., not constant) weakly $n$-harmonic map $u\in W^{1,n}(\mathbb S^n,\mathcal N)$ from $\mathbb S^n$ into $\mathcal N$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: For every $p>n$ sufficiently close to $n$, there exists a nontrivial $C^{1,\alpha}$-regular $p$-harmonic map $u_p:\mathbb S^n\to\mathcal N$ whose energies $\mathcal E_p(u_p)$ remain bounded uniformly as $p\downarrow n$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: There exists a nontrivial (i.e., not constant) $C^{1,\alpha}$-regular $n$-harmonic map $u:\mathbb S^{n+k}\to\mathcal N$ for some small positive number $\alpha>0$.

[Existence of particular solutions, \cite{CM23}]\label{thm:Qpm}
There exist forward-global radial solutions $Q^{\pm}$ to the equation \eqref{INLS} with
\[
M[Q^{\pm}] = M[Q] \quad \text{and} \quad E[Q^{\pm}] = E[Q],
\]
satisfying
\[
\|Q^{\pm}(t) - e^{it}Q\|_{H_x^{1}} \lesssim e^{-ct},
\]
for some $c>0$ and all $t>0$.

The solution $Q^{+}$ satisfies
\[
\|\nabla Q^{+}(0)\|_{L_x^{2}} > \|\nabla Q\|_{L_x^{2}},
\]
blows up in finite negative time, and satisfies $xQ^{+}\in L_x^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$.

The solution $Q^{-}$ is global, satisfies
\[
\|\nabla Q^{-}(0)\|_{L_x^{2}} < \|\nabla Q\|_{L_x^{2}},
\]
and scatters in $H_x^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ as $t\to -\infty$.
theorem.label: thm:Qpm

For unconstrained radial forward-global solutions, the argument is given in \cite[Proposition 6.1]{CM23} (see Steps 3 and 4).

\begin{thm}[Classification of threshold dynamics, \cite{CM23}]\label{thm:threshold}
Let $u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ satisfying \eqref{threshold} and $u$ be the corresponding solution of \eqref{INLS}. We have the following

\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] If
\[
\|u_{0}\|_{L_x^{2}}^{1-s_{c}} \|\nabla u_{0}\|_{L_x^{2}}^{s_{c}}
   < \|Q\|_{L_x^{2}}^{1-s_{c}} \|\nabla Q\|_{L_x^{2}}^{s_{c}},
\]
then $u$ either scatters as $t\to\pm\infty$ or $u=Q^{-}$ up to the symmetries of the equation.

\item[(ii)] If
\[
\|u_{0}\|_{L_x^{2}}^{1-s_{c}} \|\nabla u_{0}\|_{L_x^{2}}^{s_{c}}
   = \|Q\|_{L_x^{2}}^{1-s_{c}} \|\nabla Q\|_{L_x^{2}}^{s_{c}},
\]
then $u = e^{it}Q$ up to the symmetries of the equation.

\item[(iii)] If
\[
\|u_{0}\|_{L_x^{2}}^{1-s_{c}} \|\nabla u_{0}\|_{L_x^{2}}^{s_{c}}
   > \|Q\|_{L_x^{2}}^{1-s_{c}} \|\nabla Q\|_{L_x^{2}}^{s_{c}}
\]
and $u_{0}$ is radial or $xu_{0}\in L_x^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$, then $u$ either blows up in finite positive and negative times or $u=Q^{+}$ up to the symmetries of the equation.
\end{itemize}

one gets $\nabla\Delta Q\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ “precisely in the range $b\in(0,\tfrac12)$,” which allowed \cite{CM23} to control $\dot\alpha$ there.

The alternative approach described here is: since the pointwise bound on $|\dot\alpha|$ is “ultimately integrated to obtain a uniform bound on $|\alpha(t)-\alpha(s)|$,” it suffices to estimate the time integral of $|\dot\alpha|$. This is achieved by deriving “suitable Strichartz-type estimates for the function $g$,” using the equation satisfied by $g$ (cf. \eqref{solug} in the paper). This method is said to be “less sensitive to the precise decay and smoothness properties of $Q$” and can be carried out for the full range $b\in(0,1)$.
expanded_sketch:
A key ingredient in the proof of the above results is the modulation analysis, which studies solutions to
\begin{equation}\label{INLS}
\begin{cases} i\partial_t u + \Delta u + |x|^{-b}|u|^2 u = 0, \\
u(0,\cdot)=u_0(\cdot)\in H^1(\R^3),
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
while they remain close to the orbit of the ground state $e^{it}Q$. One introduces
\[
\delta(t)=\left|\int |\nabla u(t,x)|^2\,dx-\int |\nabla Q(x)|^2\,dx\right|,
\]
rescales to the threshold regime $M[u_0]=M[Q]$ and $E[u_0]=E[Q]$, and for small $\delta_0$ defines $I_0=\{t\in I:\delta(t)<\delta_0\}$. If $\delta_0$ is sufficiently small, the Implicit Function Theorem gives a phase function $\zeta:I_0\to\mathbb R$ so that
\[
 g(t)=g_1(t)+ig_2(t)=e^{-i(\zeta(t)+t)}u(t)-Q,\qquad (g_2(t),Q)=0.
\]
Then one further decomposes
\[
 g(t)=\alpha(t)Q+h(t),\qquad \alpha(t)=(g_1(t),\Delta Q)/(Q,\Delta Q),
\]
obtaining orthogonality conditions on $h(t)$ that “play a key role in the analysis.”

The restriction $b\in(0,\tfrac12)$ in \cite{CM23} is explained as coming “entirely from estimating the time derivative of the parameter $\alpha$”: using decay of $Q$ (e.g. $|\nabla Q(x)|\lesssim |Q(x)|\sim (1+|x|)^{-1}e^{-|x|}$) and a bound
\[
|\nabla\Delta Q|\lesssim |x|^{-b-1}Q^3+|x|^{-b}Q^2|\nabla Q|+|\nabla Q|,
\]
one gets $\nabla\Delta Q\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ “precisely in the range $b\in(0,\tfrac12)$,” which allowed \cite{CM23} to control $\dot\alpha$ there.

The alternative approach described here is: since the pointwise bound on $|\dot\alpha|$ is “ultimately integrated to obtain a uniform bound on $|\alpha(t)-\alpha(s)|$,” it suffices to estimate the time integral of $|\dot\alpha|$. This is achieved by deriving “suitable Strichartz-type estimates for the function $g$,” using the equation satisfied by $g$,
\begin{equation}\label{solug}
i\partial_t g + (\Delta-1) g  - \dot\zeta (g+Q) + R(g) = 0,
\end{equation}
rather than merely referring to the equation above. This method is said to be “less sensitive to the precise decay and smoothness properties of $Q$” and can be carried out for the full range $b\in(0,1)$.,

[Existence of particular solutions, \cite{CM23}]\label{thm:Qpm}
There exist forward-global radial solutions $Q^{\pm}$ to the equation \begin{equation}\label{INLS}
\begin{cases} i\partial_t u + \Delta u + |x|^{-b}|u|^2 u = 0, \\
u(0,\cdot)=u_0(\cdot)\in H^1(\R^3),
\end{cases}
\end{equation} with
\[
M[Q^{\pm}] = M[Q] \quad \text{and} \quad E[Q^{\pm}] = E[Q],
\]
satisfying
\[
\|Q^{\pm}(t) - e^{it}Q\|_{H_x^{1}} \lesssim e^{-ct},
\]
for some $c>0$ and all $t>0$.

The solution $Q^{+}$ satisfies
\[
\|\nabla Q^{+}(0)\|_{L_x^{2}} > \|\nabla Q\|_{L_x^{2}},
\]
blows up in finite negative time, and satisfies $xQ^{+}\in L_x^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$.

The solution $Q^{-}$ is global, satisfies
\[
\|\nabla Q^{-}(0)\|_{L_x^{2}} < \|\nabla Q\|_{L_x^{2}},
\]
and scatters in $H_x^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ as $t\to -\infty$.

mcq.question:
Let $n\ge 3$ and $\Omega=B_R(0)\subset\mathbb R^n$ for some $R>0$. Let $u_0,w_0\in W^{1,\infty}(\overline\Omega)$ be positive and radially symmetric. Assume
\[
 f(|\nabla v|^2)=(1+|\nabla v|^2)^{-\frac p2},\qquad g(|\nabla z|^2)=(1+|\nabla z|^2)^{-\frac q2},
\]
with $p,q\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $p<\frac{n-2}{n-1}$ and $q<\frac{n-2}{n-1}$. Consider the system for $(u,v,w,z)$ on $\Omega\times(0,\infty)$:
\[
\begin{cases}
 u_t = \Delta u -\nabla\cdot\big(u\,f(|\nabla v|^2)\nabla v\big),\\
 0 = \Delta v - \mu_w + w,\quad \mu_w=f_{\Omega}w,\\
 w_t = \Delta w -\nabla\cdot\big(w\,g(|\nabla z|^2)\nabla z\big),\\
 0 = \Delta z - \mu_u + u,\quad \mu_u=f_{\Omega}u,\\
 \partial_\nu u=\partial_\nu v=\partial_\nu w=\partial_\nu z=0\ \text{on }\partial\Omega,\\
 u(\cdot,0)=u_0,\ w(\cdot,0)=w_0.
\end{cases}
\]
Under these assumptions, which statement asserts the existence of an object with a property guaranteeing finite-time blow-up of the corresponding solution?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
There exist functions $M_1,M_2\in C^0([0,R])$ such that, if the radially symmetric positive initial data $u_0,w_0\in W^{1,\infty}(\overline\Omega)$ satisfy
\[\int_{B_r(0)}u_0\,dx\ge M_1(r),\qquad \int_{B_r(0)}w_0\,dx\ge M_2(r)\qquad\text{for all }r\in(0,R),\]
then the corresponding solution $(u,v,w,z)$ of the above system blows up in finite time.

choices.label: B
choices.text:
There exist constants $M_1,M_2>0$ (independent of $r$) such that, if the radially symmetric positive initial data $u_0,w_0\in W^{1,\infty}(\overline\Omega)$ satisfy
\[\int_{B_r(0)}u_0\,dx\ge M_1,\qquad \int_{B_r(0)}w_0\,dx\ge M_2\qquad\text{for all }r\in(0,R),\]
then the corresponding solution $(u,v,w,z)$ of the above system blows up in finite time.

choices.label: C

There exist functions $M_1,M_2\in C^0([0,R])$ such that, if the radially symmetric positive initial data $u_0,w_0\in W^{1,\infty}(\overline\Omega)$ satisfy
\[\int_{B_R(0)}u_0\,dx\ge M_1(R),\qquad \int_{B_R(0)}w_0\,dx\ge M_2(R),\]
then the corresponding solution $(u,v,w,z)$ of the above system blows up in finite time.

choices.label: D

For every choice of $u_0,w_0\in W^{1,\infty}(\overline\Omega)$ that are positive and radially symmetric, there exist functions $M_1,M_2\in C^0([0,R])$ (possibly depending on $u_0,w_0$) such that if
\[\int_{B_r(0)}u_0\,dx\ge M_1(r),\qquad \int_{B_r(0)}w_0\,dx\ge M_2(r)\qquad\text{for all }r\in(0,R),\]

theorem.content:
[\ref{thm:aksz}]\label{thm:introaksz}
	If $Y$ is an $\mathcal{O}$-compact $d$-oriented prestack and $X$ an $n$-shifted Poisson derived Artin stack such that $\MapSt(Y,X)$ is locally of finite presentation. Then the mapping prestack
	\[\MapSt(Y,X)\]
	has a natural $(n-d)$-shifted Poisson structure.
theorem.label: thm:introaksz

post_theorem_intro_text:
\subsection*{Strategy}
\par The proof follows a similar strategy as in \cite{lagthick}. For an $n$-shifted Poisson derived scheme, it was established that it is possible to construct a formal thickening
\[X \rightarrow X^\mathrm{symp}\]
with an $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian structure on it. Conversely, such a thickening provides an $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $X$. The idea is then to apply $\MapSt(Y,\textendash)$ on this morphism, and use an AKSZ construction for Lagrangian morphisms (\cite[2.35. (2)]{sympgrpd}) to get an $(n-d+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening of $\MapSt(Y,X)$. Unfortunately, the theorem proved in \cite{lagthick} was too restrictive, because in really few cases $\MapSt(Y,X)$ is still a derived scheme. First, we extend the definition of shifted Poisson structures on $X$ for $X$ being a prestack only assumed to have a deformation theory and be locally of finite presentation, and then we extend the theorem for such an $X$. Thus proving a conjecture of Calaque (\cite[Conjecture 3.4.]{cotstack}):
\begin{thmintro}[\ref{thm:lagthick}]\label{thm:intro}
	If $X$ has a deformation theory and is locally of finite presentation, then there is an equivalence:
	\[\mathrm{Pois}(X,n) \simeq \mathrm{Lag}\mathrm{Thick}(X,n+1)\]
	between the spaces of $n$-shifted Poisson structures on $X$ and $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickenings of $X$.
\end{thmintro}
\par The AKSZ construction is then almost immediate: If $X$ has a deformation theory, is locally of finite presentation, and has an $n$-shifted Poisson structure, we extract an $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening
\[X \rightarrow X^\mathrm{symp}\]
and apply $\MapSt(Y,\textendash)$ on it:
\[f : \MapSt(Y,X) \rightarrow \MapSt(Y,X^\mathrm{symp}).\]
We get an $(n-d+1)$-shifted Lagrangian on it. Now, it is automatic to check that $\MapSt(Y,X)$ has a deformation theory. By assumption, $\MapSt(Y,X)$ is locally of finite presentation, so we can apply theorem \ref{thm:intro} in order to extract a shifted Poisson structure on $\MapSt(Y,X)$. The map $f$ may be not a formal thickening, however, we can take its formal completion. That way we get an $(n-d+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening of $\MapSt(Y,X)$ and so an $(n-d)$-shifted Poisson structure on it. The hard part actually lies in the proof of theorem \ref{thm:intro}.
\par Shifted Poisson structures on an arbitrary prestack $X$ with a cotangent complex are defined using formal localization, we view $X$ as a family over its de Rham prestack $\pi : X \rightarrow X_\mathrm{dR}$. For $\mathrm{Spec}(A)\rightarrow X_\mathrm{dR}$, we set $X_A$ to be the pullback of $\mathrm{Spec}(A)$ along $\pi$. Note that the map $\mathrm{Spec}(A) \rightarrow X_\mathrm{dR}$ induces a map $\mathrm{Spec}(A^\mathrm{red}) \rightarrow X$, so we can picture those constructions as follows:
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	\mathrm{Spec}(A^\mathrm{red}) \ar[rrd,bend left] \ar[ddr,bend right] \ar[rd, dashed]\\
	&X_A \ar[r]\ar[d] & X\ar[d,"\pi"]\\
	&\mathrm{Spec}(A)\ar[r] & X_\mathrm{dR}.,
	\arrow["\lrcorner"{anchor=center, pos=0.125}, draw=none, from=2-2, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
There exist two presheaves of complete filtered $k$-algebras on $X_\mathrm{dR}$: 
\[\calB_X(A) \mathbin{:\!=} \mathrm{DR}(\mathrm{Spec}(A^\mathrm{red})/X_A),\]
and
\[\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}}(A)\mathbin{:\!=} \mathrm{DR}(\mathrm{Spec}(A^\mathrm{red})/\mathrm{Spec}(A)).\]
We also naturally get a map $\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}}\rightarrow \calB_X$. If we forget filtrations, we have
\[(\calB_X)^u \simeq \pi_*\calO_X\]
and
\[(\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}})^u \simeq \calO_{X_\mathrm{dR}}.\]
It was then established in \cite{CPTVV} that an $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $X$ should be given by a $\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}}$-linear $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $\calB_X$:
\[\mathrm{Pois}(X,n)\mathbin{:\!=} \mathrm{Pois}(\calB_X/\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}},n).\]
There is a little technical thing to do in order to properly define $\mathrm{Pois}(\calB_X/\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}},n)$, because one wants the Poisson bracket to be compatible with filtrations. In \cite{CPTVV}, the authors use a trick by passing to ind-objects. In this paper, we establish that $\mathrm{Pois}(\calB_X/\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}},n)$ should correspond to $\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}}$-linear $n$-shifted Poisson structures on $\calB_X$ with filtration degree $-2$. Now, by construction, $\calB_X(A)$ and $\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}}(A)$ are derived foliations over $\mathrm{Spec}(A^\mathrm{red})$. We prove that, given an $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $X$, we get a compatible family of $A$-linear $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickenings $(X_A \rightarrow Y_A)$ over $\mathrm{Spec}(A)$ using \cref{prop:relthick}, a relative version of \cite[4.6]{lagthick}. This last proposition relies heavily on the fact that an $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $X$ is a $\bD_{X_\mathrm{dR}}$-linear $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $\calB_X$ of filtration degree $-2$. Explicitly, we get an object in:
\[\lim\limits_{\mathrm{Spec}(A) \rightarrow X_\mathrm{dR}} \mathrm{Lag}\mathrm{Thick}(X_A/\mathrm{Spec}(A),n+1).\]
We prove in \cref{prop:lagthickdesc} that such a family can be glued globally on $X$:
\[\lim\limits_{\mathrm{Spec}(A) \rightarrow X_\mathrm{dR}} \mathrm{Lag}\mathrm{Thick}(X_A/\mathrm{Spec}(A),n+1) \simeq \mathrm{Lag}\mathrm{Thick}(X,n+1).\]
We get that way an $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening of $X$.
\subsection*{Other things contained in this paper}
\par Thanks to the tools developed to prove theorem \ref{thm:introaksz}, we also include a few implications:
\begin{thmintro}
	If $X$ is a prestack that has a deformation theory and is locally of finite presentation, then there is an equivalence
	\[\mathrm{Pois}^\mathrm{nd}(X,n)\simeq \mathrm{Symp}(X,n)\]
	between the spaces of non-degenerate $n$-shifted Poisson structures on $X$ and the space of $n$-shifted symplectic structures on $X$.
\end{thmintro}
\par This theorem is already known when $X$ is Artin and locally of finite presentation, but here, we extend it. In particular, it applies to formal neighborhoods of morphisms of Artin stacks. We then give two interesting applications of it. The first one is about moduli of flat connections on a non-necessarily proper smooth scheme $X$. Using \cite{TP2}, we prove that on each $k$-point of
\[\mathrm{Vect}^\nabla(X),\]
the formal neighborhood has a shifted Poisson structure. The second application comes from BV formalism. We sketch a proof that given a function $S : U\rightarrow \mathbb{A}^1$ on a smooth affine scheme $U=\mathrm{Spec}(A)$, we have a $(-1)$-shifted coisotropic structure on
\[\stCrit(S) \rightarrow \mathrm{dCrit}(S)\]
the inclusion of the strict critical locus into the derived critical locus.
\subsection*{Relation with other work}
\par Another method to do the AKSZ construction is currently under investigation by Melani and Pourcelot (\cite{intpois}). Their strategy relies on integration along fibers of shifted Poisson structures, which is a more general method than what is presented here, we expect that their strategy work on any derived prestack without any extra representability assumptions.
\par We expect that we can recover from our construction known Poisson structures on moduli stacks, for instance, built in \cite{poismod1} or \cite{poismod2}. Comparsion between those two constructions is a non-trivial work and would be interesting to investigate.
sketch:
The strategy to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:introaksz} is:
\begin{itemize}
\item Use the (scheme-level) idea that an $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $X$ allows one to construct a formal thickening $X\to X^{\mathrm{symp}}$ equipped with an $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian structure, and conversely that such a thickening yields an $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $X$.
\item Since \cite{lagthick} is “too restrictive” (because “in really few cases $\MapSt(Y,X)$ is still a derived scheme”), first extend the definition of shifted Poisson structures to prestacks “only assumed to have a deformation theory and be locally of finite presentation,” and extend the Poisson/Lagrangian-thickening equivalence accordingly (Theorem~\ref{thm:intro}).
\item Given $X$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:introaksz} with an $n$-shifted Poisson structure, “extract an $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening” $X\to X^{\mathrm{symp}}$ and apply $\MapSt(Y,\textendash)$ to get
\[f:\MapSt(Y,X)\to \MapSt(Y,X^{\mathrm{symp}}).\]
Using an AKSZ construction for Lagrangian morphisms (\cite[2.35.(2)]{sympgrpd}), obtain an “$(n-d+1)$-shifted Lagrangian” on $f$.
\item Check that $\MapSt(Y,X)$ “has a deformation theory” and (by hypothesis) is “locally of finite presentation,” so apply Theorem~\ref{thm:intro} to “extract a shifted Poisson structure on $\MapSt(Y,X)$.” Since “the map $f$ may be not a formal thickening,” take its formal completion to get an “$(n-d+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening of $\MapSt(Y,X)$,” hence an “$(n-d)$-shifted Poisson structure on it.”
\item The remaining difficulty is deferred: “The hard part actually lies in the proof of theorem \ref{thm:intro},” which is approached via formal localization: view $\pi:X\to X_{\mathrm{dR}}$, define $\calB_X(A)=\mathrm{DR}(\Spec(A^{\mathrm{red}})/X_A)$ and $\bD_{X_{\mathrm{dR}}}(A)=\mathrm{DR}(\Spec(A^{\mathrm{red}})/\Spec(A))$ with $\bD_{X_{\mathrm{dR}}}\to \calB_X$, and set

with a filtration-compatibility refinement (“filtration degree $-2$”). From an $n$-shifted Poisson structure, construct a compatible family of relative $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickenings $(X_A\to Y_A)$ (via \cref{prop:relthick}), then prove these families glue:
\[\lim_{\Spec(A)\to X_{\mathrm{dR}}}\mathrm{LagThick}(X_A/\Spec(A),n+1)\simeq \mathrm{LagThick}(X,n+1),\]
producing an $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening of $X$.
\end{itemize}

The strategy to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:introaksz} is:
\begin{itemize}
\item Use the (scheme-level) idea that an $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $X$ allows one to construct a formal thickening $X\to X^{\mathrm{symp}}$ equipped with an $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian structure, and conversely that such a thickening yields an $n$-shifted Poisson structure on $X$.
\item Since \cite{lagthick} is “too restrictive” (because “in really few cases $\MapSt(Y,X)$ is still a derived scheme”), first extend the definition of shifted Poisson structures to prestacks “only assumed to have a deformation theory and be locally of finite presentation,” and extend the Poisson/Lagrangian-thickening equivalence accordingly. We first use the following theorem.

\begin{thmintro}[\ref{thm:lagthick}]\label{thm:intro}
	If $X$ has a deformation theory and is locally of finite presentation, then there is an equivalence:
	\[\Pois(X,n) \simeq \Lag\Thick(X,n+1)\]
	between the spaces of $n$-shifted Poisson structures on $X$ and $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickenings of $X$.
\end{thmintro}
\item Given $X$ as in the main theorem with an $n$-shifted Poisson structure, “extract an $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening” $X\to X^{\mathrm{symp}}$ and apply $\MapSt(Y,\textendash)$ to get
\[f:\MapSt(Y,X)\to \MapSt(Y,X^{\mathrm{symp}}).\]
Using an AKSZ construction for Lagrangian morphisms (\cite[2.35.(2)]{sympgrpd}), obtain an “$(n-d+1)$-shifted Lagrangian” on $f$.
\item Check that $\MapSt(Y,X)$ “has a deformation theory” and (by hypothesis) is “locally of finite presentation,” so apply the theorem above to “extract a shifted Poisson structure on $\MapSt(Y,X)$.” Since “the map $f$ may be not a formal thickening,” take its formal completion to get an “$(n-d+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening of $\MapSt(Y,X)$,” hence an “$(n-d)$-shifted Poisson structure on it.”
\item The remaining difficulty is deferred: “The hard part actually lies in the proof of theorem” (used above), which is approached via formal localization: view $\pi:X\to X_{\mathrm{dR}}$, define $\calB_X(A)=\mathrm{DR}(\Spec(A^{\mathrm{red}})/X_A)$ and $\bD_{X_{\mathrm{dR}}}(A)=\mathrm{DR}(\Spec(A^{\mathrm{red}})/\Spec(A))$ with $\bD_{X_{\mathrm{dR}}}\to \calB_X$, and set
\[\mathrm{Pois}(X,n):=\mathrm{Pois}(\calB_X/\bD_{X_{\mathrm{dR}}},n),\]
with a filtration-compatibility refinement (“filtration degree $-2$”). From an $n$-shifted Poisson structure, construct a compatible family of relative $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickenings $(X_A\to Y_A)$ (via the following proposition), then prove these families glue:
\[\lim_{\Spec(A)\to X_{\mathrm{dR}}}\mathrm{LagThick}(X_A/\Spec(A),n+1)\simeq \mathrm{LagThick}(X,n+1),\]
producing an $(n+1)$-shifted Lagrangian thickening of $X$.

\begin{prop}\label{prop:relthick}
	If $B \in \CAlg_k$ is of finite presentation, and $\calF \rightarrow \calG$ is a morphism in $\Fol_B$, then there is an equivalence
	\[\Pois(\calG/\calF,k[n](-2)) \simeq \Lag\Thick([\Spec(B)/\calG]/[\Spec(B)/\calF],n+1).\]
\end{prop}
\end{itemize}

mcq.question: Let $Y$ be an $\mathcal{O}$-compact $d$-oriented prestack and let $X$ be an $n$-shifted Poisson derived Artin stack. Assume that the mapping prestack $\MapSt(Y,X)$ is locally of finite presentation. Which statement asserts the existence of an additional structure guaranteed under these assumptions?
