\label{thMain}
If $G$ is an almost simple group and $H$ is a maximal subgroup of $G$,
then $H^{(10)}$ is perfect.
In addition, $H^{(9)}$ is perfect unless $H$ is a solvable maximal subgroup of the Fischer group $\mathrm{Fi}_{23}$.
theorem.label: thMain

ref_dict.exBad2:
\begin{example} \label{exBad2}
Let $X = \Aut(\POmega_8^+(3))$ and let $Y<X$ be the solvable maximal subgroup discussed above.
Let $S = (\Sym(4) \wr_4 \Sym(4)) \wr C_2$ act on $32$ points,
and let $G = X \wr_{32} S$.
Then $H = Y \wr_{32} S$ is a solvable maximal subgroup of $G$.
For $g = (v,s) \in G$, since $Y^d S$ is normalized by $s$, we have
$$ H \cap H^g = Y^dS \cap (Y^dS)^{vs} = (Y^d S \cap (Y^d S)^v)^s , $$
and it follows that $\dl(H \cap H^g) = dl(H \cap H^v)$.
Now we argue as in \cite[Sec. 3.2]{Sab26}.
All set-stabilizers of $S$ have derived length at least $3$ \cite[Ex. 2.11]{Sab26}, and there is no $4$-coloring with trivial stabilizer (because already $\Sym(4) \wr_4 \Sym(4)$ on $16$ points has none).
These facts together imply that $\dl(H \cap H^g) \geq 7$ for all $g \in G$.
\end{example}
ref_dict.exBad:
\begin{example} \label{exBad}
Let $S$ be a solvable group,
and let $G = (S \wr_5 \Alt(5))'$ be the derived subgroup of the natural wreath product.
It is not difficult to see that $G = B \rtimes \Alt(5)$ is perfect,
where $B$ is a subgroup of $S^5$ of index $|S:S'|$ which contains a copy of $S$.
If $K < \Alt(5)$ is a maximal subgroup,
then $H= B \rtimes K$ is a solvable maximal subgroup of $G$ whose derived length is at least the derived length of $S$
(in particular, it can be arbitrarily large).
\end{example}

post_theorem_intro_text:
We recover \cite[Th. 1.4]{Sab26} when $H$ is solvable (and $H^{(10)}$ is trivial).
The proof of Theorem \ref{thMain} relies on the Classification of the Finite Simple Groups, which allows to split into cases where the structure of $H$ is well understood.
One of our tools is the observation that, for any normal subgroup $N$ of $H$, if both $N^{(a)}$ and $(H/N)^{(b)}$ are perfect then so is $H^{(a+b)}$ (Proposition \ref{propGDL}).

It is natural to ask whether Theorem \ref{thMain} can be extended to maximal subgroups of perfect groups. In general, the answer is no:

\begin{example} \label{exBad}
Let $S$ be a solvable group,
and let $G = (S \wr_5 \Alt(5))'$ be the derived subgroup of the natural wreath product.
It is not difficult to see that $G = B \rtimes \Alt(5)$ is perfect,
where $B$ is a subgroup of $S^5$ of index $|S:S'|$ which contains a copy of $S$.
If $K < \Alt(5)$ is a maximal subgroup,
then $H= B \rtimes K$ is a solvable maximal subgroup of $G$ whose derived length is at least the derived length of $S$
(in particular, it can be arbitrarily large).
\end{example}

However, the maximal subgroup $H$ in Example \ref{exBad} contains a large normal subgroup of $G$, which is the source of its large derived length.
In Section \ref{sec4}, we show that this is the only possible obstruction:

\begin{theorem} \label{thPrimPerf}
If $G$ is a primitive perfect group with stabilizer $H$, then $H^{(10)}$ is perfect.
In addition, $H^{(9)}$ is perfect unless $H$ is a solvable maximal subgroup of the Fischer group $\mathrm{Fi}_{23}$.
\end{theorem} 

The proof of Theorem \ref{thPrimPerf} is a combination of Theorem \ref{thMain} and the O'Nan-Scott theorem.
Generalizing \cite{LS25},
it was shown in \cite[Th. 1.5]{Sab26} that in a primitive group with solvable stabilizer, there exist two points whose pointwise stabilizer has derived length bounded by an absolute constant.
The results in this paper suggest the following further generalization to all primitive groups:

\begin{conjecture} \label{conjTwoPoints}
In every finite primitive group,
there exist two points whose pointwise stabilizer $H$ satisfies that $H^{(c)}$ is perfect,
where $c$ is an absolute constant.
\end{conjecture} 

We point out in Example \ref{exBad2} that the constant in Conjecture \ref{conjTwoPoints} is at least $7$.

\label{thm_main} Let $T>0$, and let $(\rho,v)$ be the unique classical solution to the system \eqref{lim_light} satisfying
\[
\rho\in L^\infty(0,T; \mathcal{P}\cap L^\infty(\Omega)), \quad v, \nabla \log \rho \in L^\infty(0,T; W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)) \cap W^{1,\infty}(0,T; L^\infty(\Omega)).
\]
Let $\{(f^\varepsilon, v^\varepsilon)\}_{\varepsilon > 0}$ be a family of weak entropy solutions to the equation \eqref{main1} on the time interval $[0,T]$, with initial data $\{(f^\e_0, v^\e_0)\}_{\varepsilon > 0}$ satisfying the uniform bounds
\[
\sup_{\varepsilon > 0}\left( \| |x| f^\e_0\|_{L^1} + \|f^\e_0\|_{L^1_2 \cap L \log L} +  \|v^\e_0\|_{L^2}\right) < \infty.
\]

If the initial data is  {\bf well-prepared} in the sense that
\[ 
  \mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) + \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2 \to 0 \quad \mbox{as } \varepsilon \to 0,
\] 
then we have
\begin{align*}
f^\varepsilon &\to M_{\rho, 0} \quad \mbox{in } L^\infty(0,T; L^1(\Omega \times \mathbb R^2)), \cr
  \int_{\R^2} f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\to \rho \quad \mbox{in } L^\infty(0,T; L^1(\Omega)),\cr
  \frac1\varepsilon \int_{\R^2} \xi f^\varepsilon\,d\xi  &\to \rho\left(v- \nabla \log \rho \right) \quad \mbox{in } L^1((0,T) \times \Omega),\cr
  v^\varepsilon &\to v \quad \mbox{in } L^\infty(0,T; L^2(\Omega)) \cap L^2(0,T;H^1(\Omega)).
\end{align*}
In addition, the following stability estimate holds:
\begin{align*}
&\|f^\varepsilon - M_{\rho, 0}\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^1)}^2 + \|\rho_{f^\varepsilon} - \rho\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^1)}^2 + \|v^\varepsilon - v\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^2) \cap L^2(0,T; H^1)}^2 \cr
&\quad +  \|  \frac1\varepsilon \int_{\R^2} \xi f^\varepsilon\,d\xi  - \rho\left(v- \nabla \log \rho \right)\|_{L^1((0,T) \times \Omega)}^2  \cr
 &\quad \leq C\left(  \mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) + \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\right) + C\varepsilon^2.
\end{align*}

If the initial data is \textbf{scaled well-prepared} in the sense that   
\[
{\rm d}_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\e_0}, \rho_0) \to 0  \quad \mbox{and} \quad \varepsilon^2 \left(\mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) +  \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\right) \to 0  \quad \mbox{as } \varepsilon \to 0,
\]
then we have
\begin{align*}
f^\varepsilon &\rightharpoonup M_{\rho, 0} \quad \mbox{in } L^2(0,T;\mathcal{M}(\Omega\times\mathbb R^2)) \cap L^1((0,T) \times \Omega \times \mathbb R^2), \cr
 \int_{\R^2} f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup} \rho \quad \mbox{in }  L^\infty(0,T; \mathcal{M}(\Omega))\cap L^1((0,T)\times\Omega), \cr
\frac1\varepsilon \int_{\R^2} \xi f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\rightharpoonup \rho\left(v- \nabla \log \rho \right) \quad \mbox{in } L^1((0,T) \times \Omega),\cr
v^\varepsilon &\to v \quad \text{in } L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,T)\times\Omega),
\end{align*}
up to a subsequence. Moreover, we obtain the quantitative bounds
\begin{align*}
\int_0^T {\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(f^\varepsilon, M_{\rho, 0})\,dt &\leq C{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\e_0}, \rho_0) + C\varepsilon^2 \left(\mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) +  \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\right) + C\varepsilon^2, \cr
\sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} {\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\varepsilon}(t), \rho(t)) &\leq C{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\e_0}, \rho_0) + C\varepsilon^2 \left(\mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) +  \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\right) + C\varepsilon^4.
\end{align*}
Here, the constant $C>0$ is independent of $\varepsilon>0$, depending only on the initial data, $T$, and the limiting solution $(\rho, v)$.
theorem.label: thm_main

\subsection{Scaled well-prepared case} In the scaled well-prepared setting, the initial modulated energy is not required to vanish, but only to be small at the order $\e^2$:
\[
{\rm d}_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\e_0}, \rho_0) \to 0  \quad \mbox{and} \quad \e^2 \lt(\mathscr{H}[f^\e | M_{\rho, 0}](0) +  \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\rt) \to 0  \quad \mbox{as } \e \to 0.
\]
A key point is that the dissipation built into the relative entropy structure remains effective under these conditions.

Applying Lemmas \ref{lem_gd} and \ref{lem_gd2} to the pairs $(\rho^\e,\rho)$ and $(f^\e, M_{\rho,{\rm u}_\e})$ gives the comparison estimate
\begin{align*}
&\sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} {\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho^\e(t), \rho(t))    + \int_0^T {\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(f^\e, M_{\rho, {\rm u}_\e})\,ds\cr
&\quad \leq C{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho^\e_0, \rho_0) +  C\int_0^T\intrr \frac1{f^\e}|\nabla_\xi f^\e + (\xi - u^\e) f^\e|^2\,dxd\xi ds + C\int_0^T \int_\Omega \rho^\e |u^\e - {\rm u}_\e|^2\,dxds.
\end{align*}
The two dissipation terms on the right-hand side coincide with those controlled by the relative entropy inequality. Using \eqref{rel} together with the kinetic estimate \eqref{kin_ref}, we deduce
\begin{align*}
&\int_0^T\intrr \frac1{f^\e}|\nabla_\xi f^\e + (\xi - u^\e) f^\e|^2\,dxd\xi ds +  \int_0^T \int_\Omega \rho^\e |u^\e - {\rm u}_\e|^2\,dxds\cr
&\quad \leq C\e^2 \lt(\mathscr{H}[f^\e | M_{\rho, 0}](0) + \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\rt) + C\e^4.
\end{align*}
Putting the estimates together yields
\begin{align*}
&\sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} {\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho^\e(t), \rho(t)) + \int_0^T {\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(f^\e, M_{\rho, {\rm u}_\e})\,ds \cr
&\quad \leq C{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho^\e_0, \rho_0) + C\e^2 \lt(\mathscr{H}[f^\e | M_{\rho, 0}](0) + \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\rt) + C\e^4.
\end{align*}

To transition from $M_{\rho,{\rm u}_\e}$ to the simpler Maxwellian $M_{\rho,0}$, we test against $\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega\times\R^2)$ and write
\begin{align*}
\intrr \varphi (f^\e - M_{\rho, 0})\,dxd\xi &= \intrr \varphi  (f^\e - M_{\rho, {\rm u}_\e})\,dxd\xi + \intrr \varphi  ( M_{\rho, {\rm u}_\e} - M_{\rho, 0})\,dxd\xi\cr
&=: I + II.
\end{align*}
The first term satisfies
\[
|I| \leq C{\rm d}_{\rm BL}(f^\e, M_{\rho, {\rm u}_\e}),
\]
while the shift in the Maxwellian gives, 
\[
|II| \leq C\|\rho\|_{L^1}\|{\rm u}_\e\|_{L^\infty} \leq C\e.
\]
Hence, 
\[
{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(f^\e, M_{\rho, 0}) \leq C{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(f^\e, M_{\rho, {\rm u}_\e}) + C\e^2,
\]
and integrating in time, we obtain
\[
\int_0^T {\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(f^\e, M_{\rho, 0})\,dt \leq C{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho^\e_0, \rho_0) + C\e^2 \lt(\mathscr{H}[f^\e | M_{\rho, 0}](0) + \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\rt) + C\e^2.
\]
These bounds ensure the convergence of $\rho^\e$ and $f^\e$ in the bounded Lipschitz topology. 

Next, recall from Lemmas \ref{lem:mom} and \ref{lem:kin} that $\{f^\e\}_\e$ has uniform $L\log L$ bounds and uniform moment bounds:
\[
\sup_{\e > 0}\sup_{0 \leq t \leq T}\intrr (|x| + |\xi|^2) f^\e\,dxd\xi < \infty.
\]
The $L\log L$ control implies uniform integrability of $f^\e$ in $L^1(\Omega \times \R^2)$, and the moment bounds guarantee tightness in both $x$ and $\xi$. Consequently, the family $\{f^\e\}_\e$ is weak-* compact in $L^\infty(0,T; L^1(\Omega \times \R^2))$. Combining this compactness with the BL-convergence obtained above yields
\[
f^\e \rightharpoonup M_{\rho, 0} \quad \mbox{in } L^1((0,T) \times \Omega \times \R^2) \quad \text{as } \e \to 0,
\]
up to a subsequence.  Analogously, by Lemma \ref{lem:wc}, this implies that $\rho^\e$ is relatively weakly compact in $L^\infty(0,T;L^1(\Omega))$, and combined with the BL-convergence established above, we obtain
\[
\rho^\e \overset{*}{\rightharpoonup} \rho \quad \mbox{in }  L^\infty(0,T; \mathcal{M}(\Omega))\cap L^1((0,T)\times\Omega) \quad \mbox{as } \e \to 0,
\]
up to a subsequence. 

We now turn to the scaled momentum variable $\frac1\e \rho^\e u^\e$. The modulated kinetic energy bound \eqref{kin_ref} gives
\[
\frac{1}{\e^2}\int_0^T \int_\Omega \rho^\e |u^\e|^2 \,dxdt \leq \frac2{\e^2}\int_0^T \int_\Omega \rho^\e |u^\e - {\rm u}_\e|^2\,dxdt  + \frac{2T}{\e^2} \|{\rm u}_\e\|_{L^\infty}^2 \leq C,
\]
and thus
\bq\label{bdd_mom}
 \int_0^T \int_\Omega \frac1\e|\rho^\e u^\e|\,dxdt \leq \lt(\frac{1}{\e^2}\int_0^T\int_\Omega \rho^\e |u^\e|^2\,dxds \rt)^{\frac12} \leq C
\eq
for some $C>0$ independent of $\e$. Thus, by Lemma \ref{lem:wc}, there exists $\tilde u$ such that
\bq\label{weak_con_diff}
\frac1\e \rho^\e u^\e \rightharpoonup \tilde u \quad \mbox{weakly in } L^1((0,T)\times \Omega).
\eq
To identify the weak limit $\tilde u$, we obtain from \eqref{main1} that for any $\varphi \in C_c^\infty([0,T) \times  \Omega)$
\[
\int_0^T \int_\Omega \lt(\rho^\e \pa_t \varphi + \frac1\e \rho^\e u^\e \cdot \nabla \varphi \rt) dxdt + \int_\Omega \rho^\e_0 \varphi(x,0)\,dx.
\]
We then use $\rho^\e \overset{*}{\rightharpoonup} \rho$ in $L^\infty(0,T; L^1(\Omega))$ and \eqref{weak_con_diff} to obtain
\[
\int_0^T \int_\Omega \lt(\rho \pa_t \varphi + \tilde u \cdot \nabla \varphi \rt) dxdt + \int_\Omega \rho_0 \varphi(x,0)\,dx.
\]
On the other hand, the limiting density $\rho$ satisfies
\[
\int_0^T \int_\Omega \lt(\rho \pa_t \varphi + \rho (v-\nabla \log \rho)  \cdot \nabla \varphi \rt) dxdt + \int_\Omega \rho_0 \varphi(x,0)\,dx.
\]
Subtracting the two identities gives
\[
\int_0^T \int_\Omega (\tilde u - \rho (v-\nabla \log \rho))  \cdot \nabla \varphi  \,dxdt =0 \quad \mbox{for any } \varphi \in C_c^\infty([0,T) \times \Omega),
\]
and hence
\[
\tilde u = \rho (v- \nabla \log \rho) \quad \mbox{a.e. }
\]
Consequently, we have
\[
\frac1\e \rho^\e u^\e \rightharpoonup \rho (v- \nabla \log \rho)\quad \mbox{weakly in } L^1((0,T)\times \Omega ).
\]
This identifies the weak limit of the scaled momentum.   

Finally, we address the convergence of the macroscopic velocity $v^\e$.  The uniform bounds established in Section \ref{sec_unif} guarantee that
\[
v^\e \in L^\infty(0,T;L^2(\Omega)) \cap L^2(0,T;H^1(\Omega)),
\]
with constants independent of $\e$. To extract compactness, we follow the argument of \cite[Section 4, Step 3]{GJV04}.  

Rewriting the fluid equation as
\[
\pa_t v^\e  = \Delta v^\e - (v^\e \cdot\nabla)v^\e - \nabla p^\e + \frac1\e \rho^\e u^\e - \rho^\e v^\e,
\]
each term on the right-hand side admits bounds in a negative Sobolev space.  
Indeed, $\Delta v^\e \in L^2(0,T;H^{-1}(\Omega))$, the transport term satisfies  
$(v^\e\cdot\nabla)v^\e \in L^2(0,T;W^{-1,1}(\Omega))$ due to the $L^\infty_tL^2_x$ and $L^2_tH^1_x$ bounds on $v^\e$,  
the pressure term obeys $\nabla p^\e \in L^2(0,T;W^{-1,1}(\Omega))$,  
and the drag term satisfies 
\[
\frac1\e \rho^\e u^\e - \rho^\e v^\e \in L^2(0,T;L^1(\Omega)) \subset L^2(0,T;W^{-1,1}(\Omega))
\]
by Lemma \ref{lem:mom} and estimate \eqref{bdd_mom}.

Consequently, we have
\[
\|\pa_t v^\e\|_{L^2(0,T;W^{-1,1}(\Omega))} \le C,
\]
with $C$ independent of $\e$.  

If $\Omega = \T^2$, the compact embedding
\[
H^1(\Omega) \hookrightarrow \hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega) \hookrightarrow W^{-1,1}(\Omega)
\]
allows a direct application of the Aubin--Lions lemma.  

For $\Omega=\R^2$, global compactness fails, but on every compact set $K\Subset\R^2$ one still has
\[
H^1(K) \hookrightarrow \hookrightarrow L^2(K),
\]
and $L^2(K)\hookrightarrow W^{-1,1}(K)$. Applying the Aubin--Lions lemma on $K$ and using a diagonal extraction argument as in \cite{GJV04}, we obtain
\[
v^\e \to v \quad \text{in } L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,T)\times\Omega).
\]
This localized strong compactness is precisely the ingredient needed to pass to the limit in the convective term $(v^\e \cdot\nabla)v^\e$.  Combined with the convergence of $\rho^\e$ and with the identification of the weak limit of $\frac1\e\rho^\e u^\e$ obtained earlier, this yields the desired passage to the limit in the momentum equation.

\section{Formal diffusion limit and optimal expansion rates}\label{app:op_rate}

In this appendix, we briefly outline the formal diffusive scaling of the kinetic equation in \eqref{main1}, with the purpose of identifying the optimal expansion rates for $f^\e$ and its macroscopic density
\[
\rho^\e(t,x):=\intr f^\e(t,x,\xi)\,d\xi.
\]

Throughout this appendix, we focus on the kinetic equation
\[
\pa_t f^\e + \frac1\e \xi\cdot\nabla  f^\e
= \frac1{\e^2}\nabla_\xi\cdot(\nabla_\xi f^\e + (\xi-\e v^\e)f^\e),
\]
which can be rewritten as
\[
\pa_t f^\e + \frac1\e \xi\cdot\nabla  f^\e
= \frac1{\e^2}\calL f^\e - \frac1\e \nabla_\xi\cdot(v^\e f^\e),
\quad
\calL g:=\nabla_\xi\cdot(\nabla_\xi g+\xi g).
\]
The operator $\calL$ is the classical Fokker--Planck operator in velocity, whose kernel
is spanned by the normalized Maxwellian
\[
M(\xi):=\frac1{2\pi}e^{-\frac{|\xi|^2}2}.
\]

\subsection{Hilbert expansion and first-order corrector}

We postulate the standard Hilbert expansion
\[
f^\e = f_0 + \e f_1 + \e^2 f_2 + \cdots,
\quad
v^\e = v_0 + \e v_1 + \cdots,
\]
understood purely at a formal level.
Matching powers of $\e$ in the kinetic equation yields a hierarchy of equations for
$f_k$.

At leading order $\e^{-2}$, we obtain $\calL f_0=0$, which implies that
\[
f_0(t,x,\xi)=\rho(t,x)\,M(\xi)
\]
for some scalar field $\rho(t,x)$.
At the next order $\e^{-1}$, the equation for $f_1$ reads
\[
\calL f_1 = \xi\cdot\nabla (\rho M)+\nabla_\xi\cdot(v_0\rho M).
\]
Using $\nabla_\xi M=-\xi M$ and the identity
\[
\calL(\xi_i M)=-\xi_i M,
\]
a convenient particular solution is given by
\[
f_1(t,x,\xi) =(-\xi\cdot\nabla \rho(t,x)+\rho(t,x)\,v_0(t,x)\cdot\xi)M(\xi).
\]
The solvability condition is automatically satisfied at this order, since the right-hand side lies in the orthogonal complement of $\ker\calL$. Note that this is the unique solution since $\calL$ is strongly dissipative in $\ker\calL^\perp$ (see \cite{AMTU01}). For later use, we also introduce the macroscopic flux
\[
m^\e(t,x):=\intr\xi f^\e(t,x,\xi)\,d\xi.
\]
Integrating the kinetic equation in $\xi$ yields the exact continuity relation
\[
\pa_t\rho^\e+\frac1\e\nabla \cdot m^\e=0.
\]
Expanding $m^\e$ using $f_0$ and $f_1$, and recalling that
\[
\intr\xi M\,d\xi=0, \quad \intr\xi_i\xi_j M\,d\xi=\delta_{ij},
\]
we find
\[
m^\e =\e (-\nabla \rho+\rho v_0 )+O(\e^2).
\]
Substituting this expansion into the continuity equation shows that $\rho$ formally satisfies an advection--diffusion equation driven by $v_0$.

\subsection{Formal optimal convergence rates}

We now extract the optimal expansion rates suggested by the Hilbert expansion.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Rate for $f^\e$.} The Hilbert expansion gives
\[
f^\e = f_0 + \e f_1 + \e^2 f_2 + O(\e^3).
\]
Using the explicit identifications obtained in the previous subsection,
\[
f_0=\rho M, \quad f_1= (\xi\cdot\nabla \rho+\rho\,v_0\cdot\xi )M,
\]
we obtain the first-order expansion
\[
f^\e = \rho M + \e(\xi\cdot\nabla \rho+\rho\,v_0\cdot\xi)M + O(\e^2).
\]
If one truncates the expansion at order $0$, then only the weaker approximation $f^\e=\rho M+O(\e)$ remains.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Rate for $\rho^\e$.} Integrating the Hilbert expansion in $\xi$ yields
\[
\rho^\e = \intr f_0\,d\xi + \e\intr f_1\,d\xi + \e^2\intr f_2\,d\xi + O(\e^3).
\]
Since $\intr f_0\,d\xi=\rho$ and $\intr f_1\,d\xi=0$ by oddness in $\xi$, the first-order correction cancels, and thus
\[
\rho^\e-\rho =\e^2\intr f_2\,d\xi + O(\e^3), \quad\text{hence}\quad \rho^\e=\rho+O(\e^2).
\]

In summary, the expansion predicts a first-order accurate approximation for $f^\e$ and a second-order accurate approximation for $\rho^\e$.

\section{Existence theory for the limiting system}\label{app:ext}
In this part, we discuss the existence of solutions to the limiting system \eqref{lim_light} satisfying the required regularity stated in Theorem \ref{thm_main}. Recall that the limiting system reads
\begin{align}\label{lim_light2}
\begin{aligned}
&\pa_t \rho +  \nabla  \cdot (\rho v) =   \Delta  \rho, \cr
&\pa_t v + v\cdot \nabla  v + \nabla P -  \Delta  v = 0,\cr
&\nabla \cdot v = 0.
\end{aligned}
ref_dict.app:op_rate:
\begin{aligned}
\frac1{2\e^2}\int_0^t\int_\om \rho^\e |u^\e - {\rm u}_\e|^2\,dxds &\leq \frac1{\e^2}\int_0^t \int_\om \rho^\e | ({\rm u}_\e - u^\e) - \e (v - v^\e)|^2\,dxds + \int_0^t\int_\om \rho^\e |v- v^\e|^2\,dxds\cr
&\leq \frac1{\e^2} \int_0^t\int_\om \rho^\e | ({\rm u}_\e - u^\e) - \e (v - v^\e)|^2\,dxds +  C\int_0^t\int_\om |v^\e - v|^2\,dxds \cr

\end{aligned}
\end{align}
Inserting \eqref{kin_ref} into the previous bound for the momentum density gives
 \[

and thus,
\[
\frac1\e\int_0^T\int_\Omega | \rho^\e u^\e - \rho {\rm u}_\e | \,dxdt \leq C\e + C\lt( \mathscr{H}[f^\e | M_{\rho, 0}](0) +\|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\rt)^\frac12.
\]

Hence, we conclude the desired stability and convergence estimates in the well-prepared case.

\subsection{Scaled well-prepared case} In the scaled well-prepared setting, the initial modulated energy is not required to vanish, but only to be small at the order $\e^2$:
\[

\]

\begin{align*}

&\quad \leq C{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho^\e_0, \rho_0) +  C\int_0^T\intrr \frac1{f^\e}|\nabla_\xi f^\e + (\xi - u^\e) f^\e|^2\,dxd\xi ds + C\int_0^T \int_\Omega \rho^\e |u^\e - {\rm u}_\e|^2\,dxds.
\end{align*}
The two dissipation terms on the right-hand side coincide with those controlled by the relative entropy inequality. Using \eqref{rel} together with the kinetic estimate \eqref{kin_ref}, we deduce

\[

\]
This identifies the weak limit of the scaled momentum.

\section{Formal diffusion limit and optimal expansion rates}\label{app:op_rate}

In this appendix, we briefly outline the formal diffusive scaling of the kinetic equation in \eqref{main1}, with the purpose of identifying the optimal expansion rates for $f^\e$ and its macroscopic density
\[
\rho^\e(t,x):=\intr f^\e(t,x,\xi)\,d\xi.
\]

Throughout this appendix, we focus on the kinetic equation
\[
\pa_t f^\e + \frac1\e \xi\cdot\nabla  f^\e
= \frac1{\e^2}\nabla_\xi\cdot(\nabla_\xi f^\e + (\xi-\e v^\e)f^\e),
\]
which can be rewritten as
\[
\pa_t f^\e + \frac1\e \xi\cdot\nabla  f^\e
= \frac1{\e^2}\calL f^\e - \frac1\e \nabla_\xi\cdot(v^\e f^\e),
\quad
\calL g:=\nabla_\xi\cdot(\nabla_\xi g+\xi g).
\]
The operator $\calL$ is the classical Fokker--Planck operator in velocity, whose kernel
is spanned by the normalized Maxwellian
\[
M(\xi):=\frac1{2\pi}e^{-\frac{|\xi|^2}2}.
\]

\subsection{Hilbert expansion and first-order corrector}

We postulate the standard Hilbert expansion
\[
f^\e = f_0 + \e f_1 + \e^2 f_2 + \cdots,
\quad
v^\e = v_0 + \e v_1 + \cdots,
\]
understood purely at a formal level.
Matching powers of $\e$ in the kinetic equation yields a hierarchy of equations for
$f_k$.

At leading order $\e^{-2}$, we obtain $\calL f_0=0$, which implies that
\[
f_0(t,x,\xi)=\rho(t,x)\,M(\xi)
\]
for some scalar field $\rho(t,x)$.
At the next order $\e^{-1}$, the equation for $f_1$ reads
\[
\calL f_1 = \xi\cdot\nabla (\rho M)+\nabla_\xi\cdot(v_0\rho M).
\]
Using $\nabla_\xi M=-\xi M$ and the identity
\[
\calL(\xi_i M)=-\xi_i M,
\]
a convenient particular solution is given by
\[
f_1(t,x,\xi) =(-\xi\cdot\nabla \rho(t,x)+\rho(t,x)\,v_0(t,x)\cdot\xi)M(\xi).
\]
The solvability condition is automatically satisfied at this order, since the right-hand side lies in the orthogonal complement of $\ker\calL$. Note that this is the unique solution since $\calL$ is strongly dissipative in $\ker\calL^\perp$ (see \cite{AMTU01}). For later use, we also introduce the macroscopic flux
\[
m^\e(t,x):=\intr\xi f^\e(t,x,\xi)\,d\xi.
\]
Integrating the kinetic equation in $\xi$ yields the exact continuity relation
\[
\pa_t\rho^\e+\frac1\e\nabla \cdot m^\e=0.
\]
Expanding $m^\e$ using $f_0$ and $f_1$, and recalling that
\[
\intr\xi M\,d\xi=0, \quad \intr\xi_i\xi_j M\,d\xi=\delta_{ij},
\]
we find
\[
m^\e =\e (-\nabla \rho+\rho v_0 )+O(\e^2).
\]
Substituting this expansion into the continuity equation shows that $\rho$ formally satisfies an advection--diffusion equation driven by $v_0$.

\subsection{Formal optimal convergence rates}

We now extract the optimal expansion rates suggested by the Hilbert expansion.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Rate for $f^\e$.} The Hilbert expansion gives
\[
f^\e = f_0 + \e f_1 + \e^2 f_2 + O(\e^3).
\]
Using the explicit identifications obtained in the previous subsection,
\[
f_0=\rho M, \quad f_1= (\xi\cdot\nabla \rho+\rho\,v_0\cdot\xi )M,
\]
we obtain the first-order expansion
\[
f^\e = \rho M + \e(\xi\cdot\nabla \rho+\rho\,v_0\cdot\xi)M + O(\e^2).
\]
If one truncates the expansion at order $0$, then only the weaker approximation $f^\e=\rho M+O(\e)$ remains.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Rate for $\rho^\e$.} Integrating the Hilbert expansion in $\xi$ yields
\[
\rho^\e = \intr f_0\,d\xi + \e\intr f_1\,d\xi + \e^2\intr f_2\,d\xi + O(\e^3).
\]
Since $\intr f_0\,d\xi=\rho$ and $\intr f_1\,d\xi=0$ by oddness in $\xi$, the first-order correction cancels, and thus
\[
\rho^\e-\rho =\e^2\intr f_2\,d\xi + O(\e^3), \quad\text{hence}\quad \rho^\e=\rho+O(\e^2).
\]

In summary, the expansion predicts a first-order accurate approximation for $f^\e$ and a second-order accurate approximation for $\rho^\e$.

\section{Existence theory for the limiting system}\label{app:ext}
In this part, we discuss the existence of solutions to the limiting system \eqref{lim_light} satisfying the required regularity stated in Theorem \ref{thm_main}. Recall that the limiting system reads
\begin{align}\label{lim_light2}
\begin{aligned}
&\pa_t \rho +  \nabla  \cdot (\rho v) =   \Delta  \rho, \cr
&\pa_t v + v\cdot \nabla  v + \nabla P -  \Delta  v = 0,\cr
&\nabla \cdot v = 0.
\end{aligned}

\begin{remark}\label{rmk_expan} 
 In the well-prepared regime, the quantitative convergence of all macroscopic quantities follows directly from the structure of the modulated energy.  If we write $u_f := \frac{m_f}{\rho_f}$, the algebraic decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{eq_exp}
  \int_{\R^2} f \log \frac{f}{M_{\rho, u}}\,d\xi = \int_{\R^2} f \log \frac{f}{M_{\rho_f, u_f}}\,d\xi +   \rho_f \log \frac{\rho_f}{\rho} + \frac{\rho_f}{2}|u_f - u|^2,
\end{equation}
is valid for any $\rho \in \R_+$ and $u \in \mathbb R^2$, separates the kinetic, density, and
momentum contributions in the relative entropy. Controlling the relative entropy $\mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon |M_{\rho,0}]$ therefore yields the quantitative $L^1$-convergence of $f^\varepsilon$ to $M_{\rho,0}$ and of $\rho^\varepsilon$ to $\rho$ through the Csisz\'ar--Kullback--Pinsker inequality. The same entropy dissipation also supplies a quantitative bound for the scaled momentum density $\frac1\varepsilon m_{f^\varepsilon}$ since its coercive part appears explicitly in the relative entropy dissipation. 

The convergence of the fluid velocity $v^\varepsilon$ is obtained from the fluid component of the modulated energy, which is tightly coupled with the kinetic entropy. In particular, the decay of the total modulated energy directly yields the quantitative convergence $v^\varepsilon \to v$ in the norms stated in Theorem \ref{thm_main}.
 \end{remark}

\begin{remark} 
In the scaled well-prepared case, the quantitative estimates obtained above for 
${\rm d}_{\rm BL}(f^\varepsilon,M_{\rho,0})$ and ${\rm d}_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\varepsilon},\rho)$ follow from the coercive 
structure of the relative entropy dissipation, which provides more than uniform boundedness and in fact yields an explicit convergence rate. However, the convergence of the scaled momentum density and the macroscopic velocity is of a different nature. 
The convergences
\[
\frac1\varepsilon m_{f^\varepsilon} \rightharpoonup \rho (v-\nabla\log\rho), \quad v^\varepsilon \to v
\]
follow from weak compactness arguments: the families $\{f^\varepsilon\}_\varepsilon$ and $\{\frac1\varepsilon m_{f^\varepsilon}\}_\varepsilon$ are uniformly integrable,
so that Dunford--Pettis yields weak compactness in $L^1$, and the velocity convergence relies on an 
Aubin--Lions compactness argument. 
Since these mechanisms lack coercivity, they do not provide quantitative convergence rates for 
$\frac1\varepsilon m_{f^\varepsilon}$ or $v^\varepsilon$, in contrast to the estimates available for $f^\varepsilon$ and $\rho_{f^\varepsilon}$.
\end{remark}

  \begin{remark} 
The stability estimates in Theorem \ref{thm_main} are consistent with the formal expansion
derived in Appendix \ref{app:op_rate}, and their optimality should be understood in a
variable-dependent and topology-dependent sense.

For the kinetic density $f^\varepsilon$, the estimate
\[
\|f^\varepsilon-M_{\rho,0}\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^1)}^2 \lesssim \mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0)+\|v^\e_0-v_0\|_{L^2}^2 + \varepsilon^2
\]
is already optimal. Indeed, the formal Hilbert expansion shows that
\[
f^\varepsilon= M_{\rho,0} + \varepsilon f_1 + O(\varepsilon^2),
\]
with a nontrivial first-order corrector $f_1$, so that an $O(\varepsilon^2)$ remainder is the best possible accuracy, independently of whether the initial data is well-prepared or scaled well-prepared.

For the macroscopic density $\rho_{f^\varepsilon} =\int_{\R^2} f^\varepsilon\,d\xi$, the situation is more subtle. While strong convergence in $L^1$ does not, in general, exhibit a sharp $\varepsilon^2$ rate, the scaled well-prepared regime yields an optimal second-order estimate in a weaker topology. More precisely, the quantitative bound
\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T} d_{\rm BL}^2(\rho_{f^\varepsilon}(t),\rho(t)) \lesssim d_{\rm BL}^2(\rho_{f^\e_0},\rho_0) + \varepsilon^2\left(\mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) +  \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\right)
+ \varepsilon^4
\]
is sharp in view of the formal expansion, since the first-order correction to the density vanishes identically and the leading nontrivial contribution appears at order $\varepsilon^2$; see Appendix \ref{app:op_rate}.

In this sense, the $\varepsilon^2$ rate for $\rho_{f^\varepsilon}$ is optimal when measured in a weak convergence topology, whereas for $f^\varepsilon$ the optimality already holds at the level of strong norms.
\end{remark}

 \begin{remark}
We comment on the relation between the present notion of scaled well-prepared data and the mildly well-prepared condition introduced in \cite{CJpre}. In the latter work, which treats the Vlasov--Fokker--Planck equation without fluid coupling, the relative entropy at the initial time is allowed to grow with $\varepsilon$, and the analysis accommodates regimes in which the free energy is not uniformly bounded as $\varepsilon\to0$. Such flexibility is possible because the macroscopic limit is governed solely by the kinetic relaxation mechanism.

In contrast, for the coupled Vlasov--Fokker--Planck--Navier--Stokes system considered here, the strong interaction between the kinetic and fluid components forces a uniform control of the initial entropy and fluid energy.
This requirement is inherent to the weak entropy framework and to the stability estimates used in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm_main}.
As a consequence, the type of entropy growth allowed in \cite{CJpre} cannot be incorporated into the present setting, and the scaled well-prepared condition formulated above represents the natural class of admissible initial data for the fluid-kinetic coupling under the light-particle scaling.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Organization of paper}

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec_pre} collects several analytical ingredients that will be used throughout the proof. We first introduce a weighted Trudinger--Moser inequality, which supplies the additional integrability needed to control the mixed kinetic-fluid interaction terms. We then derive a set of uniform a priori estimates, including moment and entropy bounds, and establish weak compactness properties for the macroscopic quantities associated with $f^\varepsilon$. Section \ref{sec_stab} is devoted to the stability structure of the light-particle limit. We combine BL-distance estimates with the relative entropy method to obtain a quantitative inequality that compares the kinetic-fluid system with the limiting hydrodynamic equations. In Section \ref{sec_proof}, we apply the stability framework to the well-prepared and scaled well-prepared initial data. This yields the convergence of $\rho_{f^\varepsilon}$, the scaled momentum, and the fluid velocity, and completes the proof of the main theorem. Finally, the appendices address complementary aspects of the limiting procedure. Appendix~\ref{app:op_rate} presents a formal diffusion limit and identifies the optimal expansion rates indicated by a Hilbert expansion. Appendix~\ref{app:ext} establishes the existence theory for the limiting system, including a continuation criterion and global-in-time existence on the torus, thereby justifying the regularity assumptions used in Theorem~\ref{thm_main}.

expanded_theorem:
\label{thm_main} Let $T>0$, and let $(\rho,v)$ be the unique classical solution to the system
\begin{align}\label{lim_light}
\begin{aligned}
&\pa_t \rho +  \nabla_x \cdot (\rho v) =   \Delta_x \rho, \cr
&\pa_t v + v\cdot \nabla_x v + \nabla_x P -  \Delta_x v = 0,\cr
&\nabla_x \cdot v = 0.
\end{aligned}
\end{align}
satisfying
\[
\rho\in L^\infty(0,T; \mathcal{P}\cap L^\infty(\Omega)), \quad v, \nabla \log \rho \in L^\infty(0,T; W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)) \cap W^{1,\infty}(0,T; L^\infty(\Omega)).
\]
Let $\{(f^\varepsilon, v^\varepsilon)\}_{\varepsilon > 0}$ be a family of weak entropy solutions to the equation
\begin{align}\label{main1}
\begin{aligned}
&\pa_t f^\e + \frac1\e \xi \cdot \nabla_x f^\e  = \frac1{\e^2}\nabla_\xi \cdot (  \nabla_\xi f^\e + (\xi - \e v^\e ) f^\e), \quad  (t,x,v) \in \R_+ \times \Omega \times \R^2,\cr
&\pa_t v^\e + v^\e \cdot \nabla_x v^\e + \nabla_x P^\e -  \Delta_x v^\e = \frac1\e \intr (\xi - \e v^\e)f^\e\,d\xi,\cr
&\nabla_x \cdot v^\e = 0,
\end{aligned}
\end{align}
on the time interval $[0,T]$, with initial data $\{(f^\e_0, v^\e_0)\}_{\varepsilon > 0}$ satisfying the uniform bounds
\[
\sup_{\varepsilon > 0}\left( \| |x| f^\e_0\|_{L^1} + \|f^\e_0\|_{L^1_2 \cap L \log L} +  \|v^\e_0\|_{L^2}\right) < \infty.
\]

If the initial data is  {\bf well-prepared} in the sense that
\[ 
  \mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) + \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2 \to 0 \quad \mbox{as } \varepsilon \to 0,
\] 
then we have
\begin{align*}
f^\varepsilon &\to M_{\rho, 0} \quad \mbox{in } L^\infty(0,T; L^1(\Omega \times \mathbb R^2)), \cr
  \int_{\R^2} f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\to \rho \quad \mbox{in } L^\infty(0,T; L^1(\Omega)),\cr
  \frac1\varepsilon \int_{\R^2} \xi f^\varepsilon\,d\xi  &\to \rho\left(v- \nabla \log \rho \right) \quad \mbox{in } L^1((0,T) \times \Omega),\cr
  v^\varepsilon &\to v \quad \mbox{in } L^\infty(0,T; L^2(\Omega)) \cap L^2(0,T;H^1(\Omega)).
\end{align*}
In addition, the following stability estimate holds:
\begin{align*}
&\|f^\varepsilon - M_{\rho, 0}\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^1)}^2 + \|\rho_{f^\varepsilon} - \rho\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^1)}^2 + \|v^\varepsilon - v\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^2) \cap L^2(0,T; H^1)}^2 \cr
&\quad +  \|  \frac1\varepsilon \int_{\R^2} \xi f^\varepsilon\,d\xi  - \rho\left(v- \nabla \log \rho \right)\|_{L^1((0,T) \times \Omega)}^2  \cr
 &\quad \leq C\left(  \mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) + \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\right) + C\varepsilon^2.
\end{align*}

If the initial data is \textbf{scaled well-prepared} in the sense that   
\[
{\rm d}_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\e_0}, \rho_0) \to 0  \quad \mbox{and} \quad \varepsilon^2 \left(\mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) +  \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\right) \to 0  \quad \mbox{as } \varepsilon \to 0,
\]
then we have
\begin{align*}
f^\varepsilon &\rightharpoonup M_{\rho, 0} \quad \mbox{in } L^2(0,T;\mathcal{M}(\Omega\times\mathbb R^2)) \cap L^1((0,T) \times \Omega \times \mathbb R^2), \cr
 \int_{\R^2} f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup} \rho \quad \mbox{in }  L^\infty(0,T; \mathcal{M}(\Omega))\cap L^1((0,T)\times\Omega), \cr
\frac1\varepsilon \int_{\R^2} \xi f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\rightharpoonup \rho\left(v- \nabla \log \rho \right) \quad \mbox{in } L^1((0,T) \times \Omega),\cr
v^\varepsilon &\to v \quad \text{in } L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,T)\times\Omega),
\end{align*}
up to a subsequence. Moreover, we obtain the quantitative bounds
\begin{align*}
\int_0^T {\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(f^\varepsilon, M_{\rho, 0})\,dt &\leq C{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\e_0}, \rho_0) + C\varepsilon^2 \left(\mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) +  \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\right) + C\varepsilon^2, \cr
\sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} {\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\varepsilon}(t), \rho(t)) &\leq C{\rm d}^2_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f^\e_0}, \rho_0) + C\varepsilon^2 \left(\mathscr{H}[f^\varepsilon | M_{\rho, 0}](0) +  \|v^\e_0 - v_0\|_{L^2}^2\right) + C\varepsilon^4.
\end{align*}
Here, the constant $C>0$ is independent of $\varepsilon>0$, depending only on the initial data, $T$, and the limiting solution $(\rho, v)$.

\[
\begin{cases}
\partial_t \rho + \nabla_x\cdot(\rho v)=\Delta_x\rho,\\
\partial_t v+ v\cdot\nabla_x v+\nabla_x P-\Delta_x v=0,\\
\nabla_x\cdot v=0,
\end{cases}
\]
satisfying
\[\rho\in L^\infty(0,T;\mathcal P\cap L^\infty(\Omega)),\qquad v,\nabla\log\rho\in L^\infty(0,T;W^{1,\infty}(\Omega))\cap W^{1,\infty}(0,T;L^\infty(\Omega)).\]
Let \{(f^\varepsilon,v^\varepsilon)\}_{\varepsilon>0} be weak entropy solutions on [0,T] of
\[
\begin{cases}
\partial_t f^\varepsilon+\frac1\varepsilon\,\xi\cdot\nabla_x f^\varepsilon=\frac1{\varepsilon^2}\nabla_\xi\cdot\bigl(\nabla_\xi f^\varepsilon+(\xi-\varepsilon v^\varepsilon)f^\varepsilon\bigr),\quad (t,x,\xi)\in\mathbb R_+\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^2,\\
\partial_t v^\varepsilon+v^\varepsilon\cdot\nabla_x v^\varepsilon+\nabla_x P^\varepsilon-\Delta_x v^\varepsilon=\frac1\varepsilon\int_{\mathbb R^2}(\xi-\varepsilon v^\varepsilon)f^\varepsilon\,d\xi,\\
\nabla_x\cdot v^\varepsilon=0,
\end{cases}
\]
with initial data \{(f_0^\varepsilon,v_0^\varepsilon)\}_{\varepsilon>0} satisfying
\[\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\Bigl(\||x|f_0^\varepsilon\|_{L^1}+\|f_0^\varepsilon\|_{L^1_2\cap L\log L}+\|v_0^\varepsilon\|_{L^2}\Bigr)<\infty.\]
Write \(\rho_{f^\varepsilon}:=\int_{\mathbb R^2} f^\varepsilon\,d\xi\), and let \(M_{\rho,0}\) denote the Maxwellian with density \(\rho\) and mean velocity 0. Assume either (i) the data are well-prepared, i.e.
\[\mathscr H[f^\varepsilon\mid M_{\rho,0}](0)+\|v_0^\varepsilon-v_0\|_{L^2}^2\to0\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\to0,\]
or (ii) the data are scaled well-prepared, i.e.
\[d_{\rm BL}(\rho_{f_0^\varepsilon},\rho_0)\to0\quad\text{and}\quad \varepsilon^2\Bigl(\mathscr H[f^\varepsilon\mid M_{\rho,0}](0)+\|v_0^\varepsilon-v_0\|_{L^2}^2\Bigr)\to0\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\to0.\]
Which of the following is the strongest consequence about the limit \(\varepsilon\to0\) that can be proved (including any quantitative estimates)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
If the initial data are well-prepared, then as \(\varepsilon\to0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f^\varepsilon &\to M_{\rho,0} &&\text{in }L^\infty(0,T;L^1(\Omega\times\mathbb R^2)),\\
\rho_{f^\varepsilon}=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\to \rho &&\text{in }L^\infty(0,T;L^1(\Omega)),\\
\frac1\varepsilon\int_{\mathbb R^2}\xi f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\to \rho\bigl(v-\nabla\log\rho\bigr) &&\text{in }L^1((0,T)\times\Omega),\\
v^\varepsilon &\to v &&\text{in }L^\infty(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\cap L^2(0,T;H^1(\Omega)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover, there exists \(C>0\) independent of \(\varepsilon\) such that
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\|f^\varepsilon-M_{\rho,0}\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^1(\Omega\times\mathbb R^2))}^2+\|\rho_{f^\varepsilon}-\rho\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^1(\Omega))}^2+\|v^\varepsilon-v\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\cap L^2(0,T;H^1(\Omega))}^2\\
&\quad+\left\|\frac1\varepsilon\int_{\mathbb R^2}\xi f^\varepsilon\,d\xi-\rho\bigl(v-\nabla\log\rho\bigr)\right\|_{L^1((0,T)\times\Omega)}^2
\le C\Bigl(\mathscr H[f^\varepsilon\mid M_{\rho,0}](0)+\|v_0^\varepsilon-v_0\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\Bigr)+C\varepsilon^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

If instead the initial data are scaled well-prepared, then (up to a subsequence) as \(\varepsilon\to0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f^\varepsilon &\rightharpoonup M_{\rho,0} &&\text{in }L^2(0,T;\mathcal M(\Omega\times\mathbb R^2))\cap L^1((0,T)\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^2),\\
\rho_{f^\varepsilon}=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup} \rho &&\text{in }L^\infty(0,T;\mathcal M(\Omega))\cap L^1((0,T)\times\Omega),\\
\frac1\varepsilon\int_{\mathbb R^2}\xi f^\varepsilon\,d\xi &\rightharpoonup \rho\bigl(v-\nabla\log\rho\bigr) &&\text{in }L^1((0,T)\times\Omega),\\
v^\varepsilon &\to v &&\text{in }L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,T)\times\Omega).
\end{aligned}
\]
Furthermore, there exists \(C>0\) independent of \(\varepsilon\) such that
\[

\[

\]

\[

\label{JPX} 
Let $k\geq 5$, and $a_1,\dots,a_k\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^k a_i=0$. 
Let $A\subseteq [N]$ be $K_{s,t}$-free and assume that $A$ lacks nontrivial solutions of $a_1x_1+\cdots +a_kx_k=0$. Then
\[
|A|\ll N^{1-1/s} \exp(-O_{a_i,s,t}((\log\log N)^{\frac17})).
\]
theorem.label: JPX

Let $A\subseteq [N]$ be $K_{s,t}$-free and assume that $A$ lacks nontrivial solutions of $a_1x_1+\cdots +a_kx_k=0$. Then

\]

ref_dict.JPX2:
\begin{theorem}\label{JPX2}
Let $q$ be a fixed odd prime power.  Let $k\ge 5$ and $a_1,\dots,a_k\in\F_q^\times$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^k a_i=0$.
Let $A\subseteq \F_q^n$ be $K_{s,t}$-free and assume that $A$ contains no nontrivial solution to
$a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=0$.  Then, by writing $N=q^n$, there exists $c=c(q,k,s,t)>0$ such that
\[
|A|\ll N^{1-1/s}(\log N)^{-c}.
\]
\end{theorem}

post_theorem_intro_text:
The qualitative version of this result in the case of Sidon sets (when $s=t=2$, and with $|A| = o(N^{1/2})$) was first established by Conlon, Fox, Sudakov, and Zhao~\cite{CFSZ}, who proved it using a regularity lemma for graphs with few cycles of length four. Not too long after, Prendiville developed a Fourier-analytic transference principle to show the improved quantitative bound $|A| = O\!\left(N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{-1}\right)$. This argument used an $L^{2}$-dense model theorem in the style of Helfgott and de Roton~\cite{HeRo} for Roth's theorem in the primes (originally established by Green~\cite{Gre05}). To prove Theorem~\ref{JPX}, we take a similar Fourier-analytic transference path, relying instead on an $L^{s}$-dense model theorem, in the spirit of Naslund's work~\cite{Naslund}.  

\medskip

\subsection*{Finite-field analogue.}
In Section~\ref{sec:finite-field} we study the same question in the vector space $\F_q^n$
($q$ a fixed odd prime power), where we establish the following theorem. 

\begin{theorem}\label{JPX2}
Let $q$ be a fixed odd prime power.  Let $k\ge 5$ and $a_1,\dots,a_k\in\F_q^\times$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^k a_i=0$.
Let $A\subseteq \F_q^n$ be $K_{s,t}$-free and assume that $A$ contains no nontrivial solution to
$a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=0$.  Then, by writing $N=q^n$, there exists $c=c(q,k,s,t)>0$ such that
\[
|A|\ll N^{1-1/s}(\log N)^{-c}.
\]
\end{theorem}

To obtain the polylogarithmic from Theorem~\ref{JPX2}, we take advantage of the polynomial method developments around the cap set problem~\cite{CLP17,EG}, in particular the improved bounds in the arithmetic $k$-cycle removal lemma in $\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ due to Fox, Lov\'asz, and Sauermann~\cite{FLS}.

We remark that $k\ge 5$ is optimal in the sense that if we want to avoid nontrivial solutions in any given $k$ translation invariant linear equation. For example, in the $K_{2,2}$ Sidon case, both $x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4$ ($k=4$) and $x+y=2z$ ($k=3$) are excluded by the Sidon condition.

\medskip
\subsection*{Proof ideas}\label{subsec:proof-ideas}

Our arguments follow the same overarching Fourier analytic transference principle from \cite{Prendi}: we build a \emph{dense model} for a sparse set (or weight) and then transfer a \emph{dense counting statement} back to the original object.  It is conceptually helpful to split the proof into two independent components.

\medskip
\noindent{\bf (1) Dense model step (Fourier approximation).}
Given a sparse set $A$ in the natural extremal scaling (for instance $|A|\asymp N^{1-1/s}$ for
$K_{s,t}$-free sets), we introduce a renormalized
nonnegative weight $\nu$ (e.g.\ $\nu=N^{1/s}\mathbf{1}_A$) so that
$\sum \nu$ is of order $N$.  The goal is to construct a nonnegative function $f$ with
\[
\sum f=\sum \nu
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\|\widehat f-\widehat\nu\|_\infty \ \ \text{small},
\]
while keeping some $L^s$ norm of $f$ bounded ($\sum f^s\ll N$ in the $K_{s,t}$ setting). Over the integers, the standard way to produce $f$ is to smooth by a Bohr set built from the large
spectrum; controlling the rank of this Bohr set is a key difficulty, and this step uses the $K_{s,t}$-freeness of $A$. Over $G=\F_q^n$ some of these steps will be simplified substantially, because the analogue of a Bohr set is an actual subspace.

\medskip
\noindent{\bf (2) Dense counting step (supersaturation).}
Fix a translation-invariant equation in $\mathbb{Z}[x_1, \dots, x_k]$, 
\[
a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=0,
\qquad a_i\ne0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k a_i=0,
\]
and write the associated counting functional
\[
T(h_1,\dots,h_k)
:=\sum_{a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=0}\ \prod_{i=1}^k h_i(x_i),
\qquad
T(h):=T(h,\dots,h).
\]
The dense model $f$ is built so that it behaves ``like a dense set'' from the point of view of
Fourier analysis; one then applies a dense-set input to obtain a nontrivial lower bound for
$T(f)$.  In the integer case this dense input comes from quantitative results on solutions to
translation-invariant equations in dense subsets of $[N]$ (Bloom-type bounds \cite{Bloom} and their refinements).
In the finite-field case we can instead use the arithmetic $k$-cycle removal lemma of
Fox--Lov\'asz--Sauermann \cite{FLS} (which in turn builds upon the works of Croot--Lev--Pach \cite{CLP17} and Ellenberg--Gijswijt \cite{EG}) and it yields polynomial supersaturation bounds.

\medskip
\noindent{\bf (3) Transference (telescoping + moment control).}
The final step is to compare $T(f)$ with $T(\nu_A)$.  A standard telescoping identity expands
\[
\prod_{i=1}^k f(x_i)-\prod_{i=1}^k \nu(x_i)
\]
as a sum of $k$ terms, each containing one copy of $f-\nu$ and $k-1$ copies of either $f$ or $\nu$.
To bound each resulting multilinear form we use a Fourier/H\"older estimate whose strength depends
on an available moment bound for a suitable \emph{majorant} $\omega\ge |f|+|\nu|$.
In the $K_{s,t}$-free setting, the underlying graph-freeness yields strong control on the second
moment energy $E_2$, which provides the $L^4$ Fourier bound needed for the counting lemma.
Combining the dense lower bound for $T(f)$ with the transference error bound
\[
|T(f)-T(\nu)|\ \ll\ N^{k-2}\,\|\widehat{f-\nu}\|_\infty,
\]
one concludes that $T(\nu)$ is also large.  Finally, if $A$ is assumed to have only ``trivial''
solutions, then $T(\nu)$ can be computed explicitly, which leads to an upper bound that contradicts the transferred lower bound for $N$ sufficiently large. 

\medskip

\subsection*{Notation}
For a function $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}$ with finite support, we define its Fourier transform on $\mathbb{T}$ by
\[
\widehat{f}(\alpha) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} f(n)e(-n\alpha),
\qquad \alpha\in\mathbb{T}.
\] 
The convolution of two functions on $\mathbb{Z}$ is denoted as
\[
f*g(x) = \sum_{y\in\mathbb{Z}} f(y)g(x-y).
\]
With respect to Haar probability measure on $\mathbb{T}$, define the $L^p$ norm of $F:\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{C}$ by 
\[
\|F\|_{p} =  \Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}}|F(\alpha)|^{p} \,\mathrm{d}\alpha \Big)^{\frac{1}{p}},
\qquad
\|F\|_{\infty}:= \sup_{\alpha \in \mathbb{T}} |F(\alpha)|.
\]
Throughout the paper, we write $f=O(g)$ or $f\ll g$ if there exists a positive constant $C$ such that $|f(x)|\le C g(x)$ for all $x$, and $f\asymp g$ if $f=O(g)$ and $g=O(f)$. We say $f= o(g)$ if for any $\varepsilon>0$, $|f(x)|\le \varepsilon g(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.

\medskip

theorem.content:
\label{thm:nonsingular-wdP}
Let $X$ be a nonsingular weak del Pezzo surface. If the tangent bundle $T_X$ is $(-K_X)$-slope unstable, then $X$ is either the Hirzebruch surface $\bF_n$ with $n\in\{0,1,2\}$, or $X\cong X_{n,1}, X_{n,2},$ or $X_{n,3}$ as described in Examples~\ref{eg:one_2blowup}, \ref{eg:two_2blowup}, and \ref{eg:three_2blowup}. In either case, $\mathcal{F}$ is induced by the canonical fibration $X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^1$.
theorem.label: thm:nonsingular-wdP

\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:candp} If $X$ is an $(-K_X)$-slope unstable del Pezzo surface with canonical singularities, then singularities of $X$ can only be one of the following types:
    \begin{enumerate}[$(1)$]
        \item $mA_1$ where $m=2$, $4$, or $6$,
        \item $A_1+A_2$,
        \item $2A_1+A_3$, and 
        \item $3A_1+D_4$.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

Assume that the tangent bundle $T_X$ is slope-unstable with respect to the polarization $-K_X$ (i.e. $T_X$ is $(-K_X)$-slope unstable), and let $\mathcal F\subset T_X$ be a destabilizing foliation/subsheaf. Which of the following is the strongest consequence of these assumptions about the isomorphism type of $X$ and the origin of $\mathcal F$?

correct_choice.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Necessarily $X$ is isomorphic either to a Hirzebruch surface $\mathbb F_n$ with $n\in\{0,1,2\}$, or to one of the surfaces $X_{n,1},X_{n,2},X_{n,3}$ obtained by successive $2$-blowups as in (1)--(3). Moreover, after running a $K_{\mathcal F}$-MMP, the outcome is always a Mori fiber space $f\colon Y_+\to Z_+$ with $\dim Z_+=1$, and the destabilizing foliation $\mathcal F$ is the (saturation of the) relative tangent sheaf $T_{X/\mathbb P^1}$ of the induced ruling $X\to\mathbb P^1$.

\label{thm:mainA}(Theorem~\ref{thm:asmpt-commuting}) 
    Let $G$ be a group equipped with a $G$-invariant $\sigma$-algebra $\Sigma$ and $\mu$, $\theta$ be two probability measures on $(G,\Sigma)$ such that $\theta\ll\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\mu^{*n}$ and
    \[
    \norm{\theta*\mu^{*t}-\mu^{*t}*\theta}_{TV}\to0 \text{ as } t\to\infty,
    \]
    where $*$ stands for convolution and norm is the total-variation norm. 

    Then ${H}^\infty (G,\mu)\subseteq {H}^\infty (G,\theta)$.

ref_dict.subsection:MarkovCh:
\begin{align}\label{ineq:dominated}
        \abs{\E\lesq{N_t}-h(g)}\leq\int_{G\times G}\abs{h(gxv)-h(gx)} \, d\ler{\mu^{*t}\times\theta}(x,v)
        < \varepsilon\cdot(1-\varepsilon)+2\norm{h}_\infty\cdot\varepsilon,
    \end{align}
    concluding that $\abs{\E\lesq{N_t}-h(g)}\xrightarrow{t\rightarrow\infty}0$, or in other words $\E\lesq{N_t}\xrightarrow{t\rightarrow\infty}h(g)$ as claimed.
\end{proof}

Since the martingale convergence theorem tells us that the assumption of Proposition~\ref{prop:theBasicLemma} of almost sure convergence is satisfied not just by bounded harmonic functions, but even positive harmonic functions, one could wonder whether Theorem~\ref{thm:asmpt-commuting} is extendable to them as well. Nonetheless, the answer is no -- it would fail already in the basic setup of abelian groups.

For example, for any positive integer $q$, the function $f(n)=q^{n}$, for $n\in\Z$, is $\mu_q$-harmonic for $\mu_q=\frac{q}{q+1}\delta_{-1}+\frac{1}{q+1}\delta_1$. Now, for $q_1 \ne q_2$ we will get no inclusion of positive harmonic functions, even though the measures $\mu_{q_1}$ and $\mu_{q_2}$ commute (as the group is abelian).

The failure of Theorem~\ref{thm:asmpt-commuting} for positive harmonic functions has a curious implication.
If measures $\mu$ and $\theta$ on $G$ commute, the only place at which our proof could (and hence, at least on occasion, must) fail is inequality (\ref{ineq:dominated}). What this means is the following.
Let $h$ be a positive $\mu$-harmonic function on $G$, and suppose that we start a number of independent $\mu$-random walks, say, from the identity. As time passes, for most of them, the values of $h$ start to be locally nearly constant, where by `locally', we understand the elements of the group to which the walker could transition within afew steps with high probability. Only for an increasingly more negligible fraction of the walks is this not so, but the extent to which it is not must be so large that the right-hand side of inequality~(\ref{ineq:dominated}) fails to go to 0. In other words, as time progresses and more and more $\mu$-random walks see the values of $h$ become increasingly alike in their vicinity, those fewer and fewer walks that do not must exhibit a very extreme opposite behaviour and see the nearby values of $h$ differ more and more from the value at which the walker is standing.

\subsection{General Markov chains}\label{subsection:MarkovCh}

Our proof can be generalised to the wider context of Markov chains on spaces with no algebraic structure.
Let $P\colon M\times\mathcal{F}\lora[0,1]$ be a Markov kernel on a measurable space $(M,\mathcal{F})$, and let us consider the set
\[
H^\infty(M,P)=\lers{h\colon M\rightarrow \R \ \bigg| \ h\in\ell^\infty(M,\mathcal{F}), h(x)=\int_{M}h(y)\, dP_x(y) \text{ for all } x\in M}
\]
of bounded $P$-harmonic functions on $M$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:generalMarkov}
    Let $P,Q$ be two Markov kernels on a measurable space $(M,\mathcal{F})$
    such that for every $x\in M$,
    \[
    \norm{\delta_x P^t Q-\delta_x Q P^t}_{TV}\to0 \ \text{ as } \ t\to\infty.
    \]
    Suppose further that there is $c>0$ such that for all $x\in M, A\in\mathcal{F}$,
    \[
    Q_x(A)\leq c\cdot \tilde{P}_x(A),
    \]
    where $\tilde{P}=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}P^n$.
    Then
    \[
    H^\infty(M,P)\subseteq H^\infty(M,Q),
    \]
    that is, every bounded $P$-harmonic function is also $Q$-harmonic.
\end{theorem}

For every $m\in M$, let $\ler{X_t^{(m)}}_{t=0}^\infty$ be the $P$-random walk started from $m$.
Moreover, let $\ler{Z_t^{(m)}}_{t=0}^\infty$ be obtained from $\ler{X_t^{(m)}}_{t=0}^\infty$
by $Z_t^{(m)}$ being the position of our walk after one independent $Q$-random step from $X_t^{(m)}$.

Lastly, let $\ler{W_t^{(m)}}_{t=0}^\infty$ be the $P$-random walk whose initial distribution is $Q_m=\delta_mQ$.

In terms of laws, for every $A\in\mathcal{F}$, we have
\begin{align*}
\P\ler{X_t^{(m)}\in A}&=\ler{\delta_mP^t}(A),\\
\P\ler{Z_t^{(m)}\in A}&=\ler{\delta_mP^tQ}(A),\\
\P\ler{W_t^{(m)}\in A}&=\ler{\delta_mQP^t}(A),
\end{align*}
and we denote the probability measure on $M^\N$ which is the law of the $P$-random walk $\ler{X_t^{(m)}}_{t}$ started at $m$ by $\nu_m$.

\begin{proposition}[Analogue of Proposition \ref{prop:theBasicLemma}]\label{prop:LemmaForMCh}
    Let a state $m\in M$ be fixed and suppose that there is $c>0$ such that $Q_x(A)\leq c\cdot \tilde{P}_x(A)$ for all $x\in M, A\in\mathcal{F}$.
    Let $f\colon M\lora\C$ be a measurable function such that for $\nu_m$-almost every trajectory $\ler{w_t}_t\in M^\N$, the values $f\ler{w_t}$ converge. Then
    \begin{align}\label{expr:convergence}
    f\ler{X_t^{(m)}}-f\ler{Z_t^{(m)}}\xrightarrow{t\rightarrow\infty}0 \ \ \ \ \nu_m \text{-almost surely.}     
    \end{align}

\begin{mainthm}\label{thm:mainA}(Theorem~\ref{thm:asmpt-commuting}) 
    Let $G$ be a group equipped with a $G$-invariant $\sigma$-algebra $\Sigma$ and $\mu$, $\theta$ be two probability measures on $(G,\Sigma)$ such that $\theta\ll\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\mu^{*n}$ and
    \[
    \norm{\theta*\mu^{*t}-\mu^{*t}*\theta}_{TV}\to0 \text{ as } t\to\infty,
    \]
    where $*$ stands for convolution and norm is the total-variation norm. 

    Then ${H}^\infty (G,\mu)\subseteq {H}^\infty (G,\theta)$.
\end{mainthm}
ref_dict.thm:mainB:
\begin{mainthm}\label{thm:mainB}
(Theorem~\ref{thm:TFAE}) 
    Let $G$ be a locally compact second countable group and let $\mu$ be an admissible Borel probability measure on $G$. Let $\theta$ be a Borel probability measure on $G$.
    Consider a hitting model $G \cup K$ for the Poisson boundary of $(G,\mu)$.

    Then the following are equivalent.

    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
        \item Every bounded $\mu$-harmonic function is $\theta$-harmonic: $H^{\infty}(G,\mu)\subseteq H^\infty(G,\theta).$
        \item  $\|\theta*\tilde{\mu}^{*t}-\tilde{\mu}^{*t}\|_{TV} \to 0$ where TV is the total-variation norm and $\tilde{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}(\mu+\delta_e)$.
        \item  $\theta*\mu^{*t}-\mu^{*t}\to 0$ in the weak* topology on $Prob(G\cup K)$. 
    \end{enumerate}
\end{mainthm}

post_theorem_intro_text:
In particular, if the measures actually commute ($\mu*\theta=\theta*\mu$) and are both \textit{generating}, then they share exactly the same bounded harmonic functions. In the case of a locally compact second countable group $G$, and Borel admissible probability measures $\mu$ and $\theta$ on $G$, it is shown in~\cite{BaderShalom2006} and~\cite{BjHaOppel2023} that if $\mu*\theta=\theta*\mu$ then every $(G,\mu)$-stationary action is also $(G,\theta)$-stationary, and vice versa. It can be shown using the Poisson boundary theory that in this case this statement is equivalent to the statement that $H^\infty(G,\mu)=H^\infty(G,\theta)$. However,    
    our proof is based on a careful treatment of martingales and not on the approach of group actions. This allows us to consider non-generating measures $\theta$, and using them, to conclude the aforementioned Choquet-Deny theorem for nilpotent groups.
    The main technical lemma states that asymptotically, the values of a bounded harmonic function observed by a random walk do not change if one adds an additional, constant step \textit{at the end} of the walk (Proposition~\ref{prop:theBasicLemma}).

    Thanks to our proof method, we obtain the result for the generality of asymptotic commutativity and with no restrictions on the group; it does not require local compactness or second countability. Furthermore, as often happens with martingale arguments, when treated carefully, the result actually holds for general Markov chains, after making the correct adaptations to the statement. We discuss these and the more general proof in Subsection~\ref{subsection:MarkovCh}.

While asymptotic commutativity is a sufficient condition for inclusion, it is not a necessary one -- see Example~\ref{example}. The correct if-and-only-if condition is ``$\mu$ being asymptotically $\theta$-invariant''. But in what sense?
We bring here a classical result of Derriennic, Theorem~\ref{thm:Derriennic}, which shows that this asymptotic invariance can be taken in the total-variation norm -- \textit{(2)} in Theorem~\ref{thm:mainB}. We translate Derriennic's proof, which holds for general Markov chains, from French in the appendix, and add a dynamical characterisation, in which the asymptotic invariance can be taken in the weak* sense -- \textit{(3)} in Theorem~\ref{thm:mainB}. For that, one should be careful about the underlying topology. We show in Lemma~\ref{lemma:hitting}  that one can use weak* topology whenever  Poisson boundary is realized as a ``hitting measure'' of the random walk. Furthermore, we show in Section~\ref{Sec:hitting} that such models exist for every admissible measure on a locally compact second countable group.
This last result, showing that $\mu$-boundaries can be realised as hitting measures, might be of independent interest for stationary theory.

This discussion is summarised by the following theorem.

\begin{mainthm}\label{thm:mainB}
(Theorem~\ref{thm:TFAE}) 
    Let $G$ be a locally compact second countable group and let $\mu$ be an admissible Borel probability measure on $G$. Let $\theta$ be a Borel probability measure on $G$.
    Consider a hitting model $G \cup K$ for the Poisson boundary of $(G,\mu)$.

    Then the following are equivalent.

    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
        \item Every bounded $\mu$-harmonic function is $\theta$-harmonic: $H^{\infty}(G,\mu)\subseteq H^\infty(G,\theta).$
        \item  $\|\theta*\tilde{\mu}^{*t}-\tilde{\mu}^{*t}\|_{TV} \to 0$ where TV is the total-variation norm and $\tilde{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}(\mu+\delta_e)$.
        \item  $\theta*\mu^{*t}-\mu^{*t}\to 0$ in the weak* topology on $Prob(G\cup K)$. 
    \end{enumerate}
\end{mainthm}

This is another manifestation of the differences between the two approaches to studying bounded harmonic functions. The proof of the ergodic characterisation is softer but is restricted only to random walks on groups, whereas the probabilistic one applies to general Markov chains. Note that in Theorem~\ref{thm:mainA} we allow an arbitrary $G$-invariant $\sigma$-algebra, whereas in Theorem~\ref{thm:mainB} we restrict to the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, since we address ergodic considerations.
But even if it was not for this greater generality of the setup, Theorem~\ref{thm:mainA} does not follow at once from Theorem~\ref{thm:mainB}, and we are as of now only able to show that $\|\theta*\tilde{\mu}^{*t}-\tilde{\mu}^{*t}\|_{TV} \to 0$ implies $\norm{\theta*\mu^{*t}-\mu^{*t}*\theta}_{TV}\to0$ by combining the two main theorems.

We remark that it is essential to consider \emph{bounded} harmonic functions throughout the discussion. While the martingale convergence theorem holds for positive functions too, even abelian groups - on which any two measures commute - admit random walks with non-constant positive harmonic functions, and generally without inclusions between the corresponding spaces of positive harmonic functions, see for example~\cite{SawyerMartinBoundary}.

Let $G$ be a group equipped with a $G$-invariant $\sigma$-algebra $\Sigma$. Let $\mu$ and $\theta$ be probability measures on $(G,\Sigma)$ such that
1) $\theta\ll \sum_{n\ge 0}\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\,\mu^{*n}$, and

theorem.content:
Let $(X,S,\lambda)$ be a mixing Anosov diffeomorphism with a Gibbs measure $\lambda$ corresponding to a H\"older continuous potential $\psi$, let $\varphi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be an aperiodic H\"older continuous cocycle  satysfying $\int \varphi=0$ and let $K_t^{\gamma,\alpha}$ be a Kochergin flow on $(\mathbb{T}^2,\nu)$ with exponent $\gamma<1/2$. Then for a.e. $\alpha\in [0,1)$ the skew product 
    $$T(x,z)=S^{K_t^{\gamma,\alpha}}_\varphi(x,z)=(S(x),K^{\gamma,\alpha}_{\varphi(x)}(z)) $$ on $(X\times \mathbb{T}^2,\lambda\times\nu)$ is Bernoulli.

post_theorem_intro_text:
It is known \cite{1} that Anosov diffeomorphisms admit Markov partitions i.e. there exists a mixing subshift of finite type with an invariant measure $(\Sigma,\sigma,\mu)$ and a H\"older continuous $\pi:\Sigma\rightarrow X$, which is an isomorphism between the two measure preserving dynamical systems. Then if $\lambda$ is the Gibbs measure corresponding to $\psi$, it follows that $\mu$ is the Gibbs measure corresponding to $\psi\circ\pi$. Therefore in order to prove Theorem $1.1$ it is enough to prove the following

\begin{theorem}
    Let $(\Sigma,\sigma,\mu)$ be a mixing subshift of finite type with a Gibbs measure $\mu$ corresponding to some H\"older continuous potential, let $\varphi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be an aperiodic H\"older continuous cocycle  satysfying $\int \varphi=0$ and let $K_t^{\gamma,\alpha}$ be a Kochergin flow with exponent $\gamma<1/2$. Then for a.e. $\alpha\in [0,1)$ the skew product
    $$T(x,z)=\sigma^{K_t^{\gamma,\alpha}}_\varphi(x,z)=(\sigma(x),K^{\gamma,\alpha}_{\varphi(x)}(z)) $$ on $(\Sigma\times \mathbb{T}^2,\mu\times\nu)$ is Bernoulli.
\end{theorem}

We focus on proving this theorem in the rest of the paper.
\paragraph{Outline of the proof}
Following \cite{16}, we reduce the proof of Bernoullicity to finding a generating VWB (very weakly Bernoulli) partition. We specify the generating partition $\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{Q}$ in Section 2.5, in fact our proof works for any smooth (satisfying \eqref{smpart}) partition $\mathcal{Q}$ of the fiber and so the main part is the proof of the VWB property. By the definition, it means that we want to find a matching between most atoms of the past partition $\bigvee_{i=0}^\infty T^i(\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{Q})$. By property \eqref{smpart} and the fact that the fiber entropy is 0, we see by Lemma 2.11, that all we need is to find a measurable isomorphism between most of the unstable sets $\Phi:\Sigma^+(x)\rightarrow\Sigma^+(\bar x)$ in the base, which would cause the fiber coordinates of $T^i(x,z)$ and $T^i(\Phi(x),\bar z)$ to stay close to each other for most of the times $i$ in some future interval $[1,N]$.

In most examples VWB has been established by constructing a matching which would bring two points close enough in time $o(N)$ to ensure that for the remaining $N-o(N)$ times in the future interval $[1,N]$ they would stay close together. In the case of skew products over SFTs this corresponds to finding the right matching between blocks of size $o(N)$ and then copying the remaining $N-o(N)$ symbols.

The situation gets more complicated in Theorem 1.2 and interestingly it requires a matching with $\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{Q}$ names of $\{T^i(x,z)\}_{i=1}^N$ and $\{T^i(\Phi(x),\bar z)\}_{i=1}^N$ agreeing on a family of disjoint short intervals of $i$, each of length $o(N)$.

Indeed, even with the assumption of good equidistribution in the fiber given by the slow growth of denominators \eqref{lancuch} of the rotation angle in the Kochergin flow, the time it takes to bring two typical points in the fiber $\frac{1}{N}$-close together is roughly of size $N$. On the other hand, the Denjoy-Koksma inequality tells us that two points which are $\frac{1}{N}$ apart in the horizontal direction in the fiber can only travel together in the direction of the flow for a distance bounded by $N^{\frac{2}{3}+\epsilon}$ before getting separated, if the exponent $\gamma$ is close to $\frac{1}{2}$.

The idea is therefore to construct the matching one block at a time and to carefully calculate the maximal measure of the domain on which it is possible to shift the Birkhoff sums of the cocycle $S_n\varphi$ by some time $t$. Obtaining the optimal measure, equal to $\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}$, involves studying various limit theorems for conditional measures on the unstable sets $\Sigma^+(x)$ and we dedicate the whole Section 3. to that matter.

Then we may hope to adjust the two trajectories with the use of the next block and $t$ chosen to be the distance by which our two points have separated by the time the previous block ends. Section 4 gives upper bounds on these distances.

In Section 5 we construct the final matching using Lemma \ref{32final} on blocks of varying length, that is with different $n$. The idea is to fix a finite set of lengths ($H_i(N),\ i=1,\dots,k$) and always use Lemma \ref{32final} with $n=H_i(N)$ for some $i$ and $t$ such that the loss of measure, which is roughly $\frac{t}{\sqrt{H_i(N)}}$, does not exceed the number of blocks of length $H_i(N)$ in our whole future interval $[1,N]$. In fact making sure the loss of measure for each such partial matching defined on a block at level $i$ (that is of length $H_i(N)$) is $o(\frac{L(N)}{H_i(N)})$, we obtain Lemma \ref{52good}, which guarantees that the matching shifts the Birkhoff sums in a controlled way (we fall into the set of good control from Lemma \ref{32final} at every step of the construction) for most words in $\Sigma^+(x)$. In Lemma \ref{52mapworks} we use the lemmas from Section 4 to bound the distances between our two points at the end of each block. Finally, in Lemma \ref{52precel} we show that for most words in $\Sigma^+(x)$ most of the interval $[1,L(N)]$ in our construction is covered by the shortest blocks (at level $k$) where the Birkhoff sums of the cocycle $\varphi$ can be bounded by $N^{\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2\eta}{10}}$ which suffices for $o(1)$ separation in the direction of the flow.

I would like to thank Adam Kanigowski for suggesting the topic as well as many helpful discussions. I am also grateful to Dmitry Dolgopyat for providing useful references and Kosma Kasprzak for detailed reading and feedback on a preliminary version of this paper.

Let $(X,S,\lambda)$ be a mixing Anosov diffeomorphism with a Gibbs measure $\lambda$ corresponding to a H\"older continuous potential $\psi$, let $\varphi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be an aperiodic H\"older continuous cocycle  satysfying $\int \varphi=0$ and let $K_t^{\gamma,\alpha}$ be a Kochergin flow on $(\mathbb{T}^2,\nu)$ with exponent $\gamma<1/2$. Then for a.e. $\alpha\in [0,1)$ the skew product 
    $$T(x,z)=S^{K_t^{\gamma,\alpha}}_\varphi(x,z)=(S(x),K^{\gamma,\alpha}_{\varphi(x)}(z)) $$ on $(X\times \mathbb{T}^2,\lambda\times\nu)$ is Bernoulli.

mcq.question:
Let $(X,S,\lambda)$ be a mixing Anosov diffeomorphism with a Gibbs measure $\lambda$ corresponding to a H\"older continuous potential $\psi$. Let $\varphi:X\to\mathbb{R}$ be an aperiodic H\"older continuous cocycle satisfying $\int_X \varphi\,d\lambda=0$. Let $K_t^{\gamma,\alpha}$ be a Kochergin flow on $(\mathbb{T}^2,\nu)$ with exponent $\gamma<\tfrac12$. For $\alpha\in[0,1)$ define the skew product on $(X\times\mathbb{T}^2,\lambda\times\nu)$ by
\[
T(x,z)=S^{K_t^{\gamma,\alpha}}_{\varphi}(x,z)=(S(x),\,K^{\gamma,\alpha}_{\varphi(x)}(z)).
\]
What is the strongest statement that can be proved about $T$ (as a measure-preserving transformation) for Lebesgue-a.e. $\alpha\in[0,1)$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: For Lebesgue-a.e. $\alpha\in[0,1)$, the skew product transformation $T(x,z)=(S(x),K^{\gamma,\alpha}_{\varphi(x)}(z))$ on $(X\times\mathbb{T}^2,\lambda\times\nu)$ is Bernoulli.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For Lebesgue-a.e. $\alpha\in[0,1)$, the skew product transformation $T(x,z)=(S(x),K^{\gamma,\alpha}_{\varphi(x)}(z))$ on $(X\times\mathbb{T}^2,\lambda\times\nu)$ is Bernoulli, and moreover the product partition $\mathcal P\times\mathcal Q$ is very weakly Bernoulli (VWB) for \emph{every} finite measurable partition $\mathcal Q$ of $\mathbb T^2$ (with no regularity assumption such as $\nu(V_\delta(\partial\mathcal Q))\to0$).

choices.label: C
choices.text: For Lebesgue-a.e. $\alpha\in[0,1)$, the skew product transformation $T(x,z)=(S(x),K^{\gamma,\alpha}_{\varphi(x)}(z))$ on $(X\times\mathbb{T}^2,\lambda\times\nu)$ is a $K$-automorphism (i.e. has completely positive entropy).

choices.label: D
choices.text: For Lebesgue-a.e. $\alpha\in[0,1)$ and for every H\"older cocycle $\varphi:X\to\mathbb R$ with $\int_X\varphi\,d\lambda=0$ (dropping the aperiodicity assumption), the skew product $T(x,z)=(S(x),K^{\gamma,\alpha}_{\varphi(x)}(z))$ on $(X\times\mathbb{T}^2,\lambda\times\nu)$ is Bernoulli.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For Lebesgue-a.e. $\alpha\in[0,1)$, the skew product $T(x,z)=(S(x),K^{\gamma,\alpha}_{\varphi(x)}(z))$ is Bernoulli for every Kochergin exponent $\gamma<1$ (in particular allowing $\gamma\ge\tfrac12$) under the same assumptions on $(X,S,\lambda)$ and on the H\"older cocycle $\varphi$.

post_theorem_intro_text:
The algorithms in Theorem \ref{thm:mainresults} have been implemented in Magma \cite{Ang25} and bug-tested against existing implementations of $ L(E, s) $ and $ L(E, \chi, s) $. The proof of (1) is elementary and only uses properties of formal power series. The proofs of (2) and (3) use a generalisation of (1), and are heavily inspired by the algorithm of Comeau-Lapointe--David--Lal\'in--Li for $ L(E, \chi, s) $ \cite[Section 5.1]{CLDLL22}, although their analogue of (1) is an ad-hoc computation using Legendre symbols.

Section \ref{sec:adicrepresentations} reviews some useful background on invariants associated to $ \rho_\lambda $, including $ \mathcal{L}(\rho_\lambda, T) $ and $ \epsilon(\rho_\lambda) $, which are sometimes implicit in the literature without good references. Section \ref{sec:computingfunctions} details Theorem \ref{thm:mainresults} and briefly justifies their running time complexities. Section \ref{sec:examplecomputations} works them out by hand for explicit examples of elliptic curves, Dirichlet characters, and other motivic objects.

ref_dict.def:Hc:
\begin{definition}\label{def:Hc} Let $(\mA_n)_n$, $\mA$ in $\Mab$. Then $(\mA_n)_n$ is said to \textbf{$H$-converge} to $\mA$ ($\mA_n \stackrel{H}{\longrightarrow} \mA$), if for all $f\in {\rm H}^{-1}(\Omega)$ and $u_n \in {\rm H}_0^1(\Omega)$ such that
\[
    -\dive (\mA_n\nabla u_n) = f,
\]
we obtain for $u\in {\rm H}^1_0(\Omega)$, satisfying
\[
  -\dive (\mA\nabla u) = f,
\]
$u_n \xrightharpoonup{ {\rm H}^1_0(\Omega)} u$ and $\mA_n \nabla u_n\xrightharpoonup{ \Ld\Omega^d} \mA \nabla u$.
\end{definition}
ref_dict.def:Hsc:
\begin{definition}\label{def:Hsc} Let $(\mA_n)_n$, $\mA$ in $\MabR$. Then $(\mA_n)_n$ is said to \textbf{$H^s$-converge} to $\mA$ ($\mA_n \stackrel{H^s}{\longrightarrow} \mA$), if for all $f\in {\rm H}^{-s}(\Omega)$ and $u_n \in {\rm H}_0^s(\Omega)$ such that
\[
    -\divs (\mA_n\grads u_n) = f,
\]we obtain for $u\in {\rm H}_0^s(\Omega)$, satisfying
\[
  -\divs (\mA\grads u) = f,
\]
$u_n \xrightharpoonup{{\rm H}_0^s(\Omega)} u$ and $\mA_n \grads u_n\xrightharpoonup{{\rm L}^2(\R^d)^d} \mA \grads u$.
\end{definition}

mcq.question: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ have boundary of Lebesgue measure zero, with $d\ge 1$ and $s\in(0,1)$. Let $(\mathcal A_n)_n$ and $\mathcal A$ belong to $\mathcal M(\alpha,\beta;\mathbb{R}^d)$. What is the strongest statement that can be proved relating the convergence $\mathcal A_n\stackrel{H^s}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal A$ to the behavior of the restrictions $\mathcal A_n|_\Omega$ and $\mathcal A_n|_{\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\overline\Omega}$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: $$\mathcal A_n\stackrel{H^s}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal A_n|_\Omega\stackrel{H}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal A|_\Omega\ \text{ and }\ \mathcal A_n|_{\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\overline\Omega}\xrightharpoonup{\ *\ }\mathcal A|_{\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\overline\Omega},$$ where $\xrightharpoonup{*}$ denotes weak-$*$ convergence in ${\rm L}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\overline\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d\times d})$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: $$\mathcal A_n\stackrel{H^s}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal A_n|_\Omega\stackrel{H}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal A|_\Omega\ \text{ and }\ \mathcal A_n|_{\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\overline\Omega}\to \mathcal A|_{\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\overline\Omega}\ \text{strongly in }{\rm L}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\overline\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}).$$

choices.label: C

theorem.content:
\label{t1}
		Let $\Omega$ be a bounded non-convex polygonal domain, $\Omega^*$ be a bounded convex domain in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and $u$ be an Alexandrov solution to \eqref{be1}. If $\frac{1}{\lambda} \leq f, g \leq \lambda$ within $\Omega$ and $\Omega^*$, respectively, for some positive constant $\lambda$, then $u\in W^{2, 1+\epsilon}(\overline{\Omega}).$
theorem.label: t1

post_theorem_intro_text:
With the convexity of \(\Omega\), Caffarelli proved the doubling property of the Monge-Ampère measure associated with the potential function \(u\). In the case of a non-convex polygonal source domain, the doubling property may fail for a general convex set centered at some point in the closure of the domain. It is crucial to first establish the following doubling property for sections with small height.
	\begin{proposition}\label{doubling property}
		Under the same assumptions as in Theorem \ref{t1}, there exists a constant $h_0$ that depends on the geometry of $\Omega$ such that, for any $x \in \Omega$, we have
		$$|\nabla u(S^c_h(x))| \leq C |\nabla u\left(\frac{1}{2} S^c_h(x)\right)|,$$
		for some universal constant $C > 0$ and for all $h < h_0$.
	\end{proposition}

	The key to proving the above doubling property is to show that the sections are well localized. Specifically, any section centered in $\overline{\Omega}$ will be sufficiently small if its height is small. Once the sections are localized, the area of $S^c_h(x) \cap \Omega$ near the concave vertex is a positive portion of the area of $S^c_h(x)$, from which the doubling property follows.  

	Another issue to address is that near the concave vertex, it is not clear whether the engulfing property holds for all centered sections. Our strategy is to decompose the domain near this vertex into two sets and prove that the intersections of sections with each set satisfy the engulfing property.  

	The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce some notation and preliminaries. Section 3 is devoted to the proof of the doubling property, specifically Proposition \ref{doubling property}. In the final section, we complete the proof of Theorem \ref{t1}.
sketch:
To prove Theorem~\ref{t1}, the introduction highlights two main issues and the corresponding strategy.

1) **Establish a doubling property adapted to non-convex polygonal domains.** Since for non-convex polygonal source domains “the doubling property may fail for a general convex set centered at some point in the closure of the domain,” it is “crucial to first establish” a doubling property specifically “for sections with small height,” namely Proposition~\ref{doubling property}.

2) **Prove the doubling property via localization of sections.** “The key to proving the above doubling property is to show that the sections are well localized. Specifically, any section centered in $\overline{\Omega}$ will be sufficiently small if its height is small.” “Once the sections are localized,” one shows that “the area of $S^c_h(x)\cap\Omega$ near the concave vertex is a positive portion of the area of $S^c_h(x)$, from which the doubling property follows.”

3) **Handle the engulfing issue near the concave vertex by domain decomposition.** Near the concave vertex, “it is not clear whether the engulfing property holds for all centered sections,” so the strategy is “to decompose the domain near this vertex into two sets and prove that the intersections of sections with each set satisfy the engulfing property.”

Finally, after proving Proposition~\ref{doubling property} (Section 3), “in the final section, we complete the proof of Theorem~\ref{t1}.”

mcq.question:
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded non-convex polygonal domain, let $\Omega^*\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded convex domain, and let $u$ be an Alexandrov solution of
\[
(\nabla u)_\sharp f = g.
\]
Assume there exists a constant $\lambda>0$ such that
\[
\frac{1}{\lambda}\le f\le \lambda \quad\text{in }\Omega,\qquad \frac{1}{\lambda}\le g\le \lambda \quad\text{in }\Omega^*.
\]
What is the strongest regularity statement that can be proved for $u$ under these assumptions?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $u\in W^{2,1+\varepsilon}(\overline{\Omega}).$

choices.label: B
choices.text: There exists $varepsilon>0$ such that $u\in W^{2,1+\varepsilon}(\Omega)$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $u\in W^{2,1+\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that $u\in W^{2,1+C}(\overline{\Omega})$ (i.e. one can take $\varepsilon=C$ depending only on the dimension).

choices.label: E
choices.text: There exists $h_0>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that, for every $x\in\overline{\Omega}$ and every $h<h_0$, the centered section $S_h^c(x)$ satisfies a uniform engulfing property and consequently $u\in W^{2,1+\varepsilon}(\overline{\Omega})$ without any domain decomposition near concave vertices.

TAS.justification: It is not a mere restatement of a named theorem; it asks for the strongest provable regularity given competing global/boundary/local variants and dependence of the exponent. The non-convexity and polygonal boundary create genuine alternatives (interior vs up to boundary, decomposition near concave vertices).

GPS.justification: Selecting the strongest valid statement requires knowing (or reasoning about) how non-convexity/concave corners obstruct boundary regularity and global estimates, while interior W^{2,1+ε} can still hold. One must compare subtle distinctions: Ω vs \bar{Ω}, local vs global, and whether ε is universal.

DQS.justification: Distractors are plausible and target common failure modes: (B) incorrectly upgrading to global-in-Ω when boundary singularities may intervene; (C) is a weaker true alternative (good near-miss); (D) wrongly claims a universal exponent independent of geometry; (E) asserts a strong geometric engulfing property known to fail near concave vertices without decomposition. Choices are distinct and aligned with typical misconceptions in Monge–Ampère regularity.
